title: Beyond tessellation: AI-derived choroidal vessel density on multi-channel cSLO as a surrogate biomarker for OCT choroidal parameters.
abstract: Purpose To develop an AI-based method for quantifying choroidal vessel density (CVD) from ultra-widefield confocal scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (UWF-cSLO) and to validate this metric against swept-source optical coherence tomography (SS-OCT) choroidal parameters. Methods In this retrospective cross-sectional study, 633 eyes from 354 participants underwent simultaneous UWF-cSLO and SS-OCT imaging on an integrated platform, ensuring precise spatial co-registration. A TransUNet deep-learning model segmented choroidal vessels from red-channel (R; 665 nm) and infrared-channel (IR; 785 nm) images, yielding channel-specific metrics (R-CVD and IR-CVD) and a combined metric (IR + R CVD). Eight SS-OCT parameters-including choroidal thickness (CT), choroidal vascularity index (CVI), luminal area, stromal area (SA), total choroidal area (TCA), and vessel volume index (VVI)-served as reference measures. Associations were evaluated using Spearman correlations with participant-level clustered bootstrap confidence intervals, multivariable generalised estimating equations (GEE) adjusted for age and sex, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Results Segmentation accuracy exceeded 0.95 (Dice coefficient) in both channels. R-CVD exhibited the strongest inverse correlations with structural and volumetric OCT parameters (SA: ρ = -0.619; CT: ρ = -0.615; TCA: ρ = -0.615; all q < 0.001), whereas IR + R CVD correlated most closely with proportion-based indices (VVI: ρ = -0.34; CVI: ρ = -0.29). These channel-dependent patterns persisted after adjustment for age and sex in multivariable GEE models. On ROC analysis, R-CVD discriminated thin from thick choroids with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.789 (sensitivity 72.5%; specificity 74.8%), whereas IR-CVD alone showed near-chance performance (AUC 0.517). Conclusions AI-derived CVD from UWF-cSLO correlates strongly with SS-OCT choroidal parameters in a wavelength-dependent manner and may serve as an accessible surrogate for choroidal structural assessment in settings without OCT.

title: From MRI-defined bone marrow lesions to pain, structural progression, and subchondral remodeling in knee osteoarthritis: an integrated multi-database bibliometric and text-mining analysis.
abstract: Objective To characterize the publication landscape, intellectual structure, thematic evolution, and emerging clinical, mechanistic, and translational directions of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-defined bone marrow lesion (BML) research in knee osteoarthritis. Methods Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, and PubMed were searched using core concepts related to knee osteoarthritis, MRI, and BMLs or bone marrow edema-like lesions. The searches initially identified 2,452 records, of which 2,415 were exported after database-level filters. Following cross-database deduplication, eligibility assessment, and application of the prespecified publication cutoff, 726 publications constituted the final integrated corpus. Descriptive bibliometrics, collaboration-network analysis, reference co-citation analysis, keyword and MeSH mapping, temporal thematic analysis, term frequency-inverse document frequency-based document clustering, and dictionary-based bridge-theme mapping were performed. Candidate cluster solutions from k = 2 to k = 10 were evaluated using within-cluster sum of squares, silhouette width, gap statistics, and repeated-subsample stability. Results Publication activity increased substantially from 1996 through 2025, with the partial 2026 count reflecting publications available by June 1. Osteoarthritis and Cartilage was the leading journal, and the United States, Australia, Germany, China, and the United Kingdom were the major contributing countries. The knowledge base was anchored by studies of whole-joint MRI assessment, BML-related pain, structural progression, and imaging-pathology interpretation. Six exploratory text-derived research domains were identified: post-traumatic and surgical BML outcomes; community-based structural and risk correlates; subchondral biology, biomarkers, and mechanisms; longitudinal whole-joint progression and symptoms; pharmacologic, biologic, and interventional treatment; and MRI quantification and methodological validation. No single diagnostic identified a uniquely optimal cluster number; the six-domain solution was retained as an interpretable intermediate-granularity representation with moderate resampling stability. Exclusion of the 28 publications dated 2026 did not materially alter the publication trajectory, leading recent terms, or temporal-theme prevalence. Conclusion MRI-defined BML research in knee osteoarthritis has developed into a multidisciplinary field connecting imaging phenotypes with symptoms, structural progression, subchondral remodeling, biomechanics, inflammation, and treatment-oriented investigation. Future studies should integrate longitudinal lesion trajectories, quantitative imaging, adjacent joint pathology, biomechanical measures, biological markers, and pain phenotyping to clarify clinically meaningful BML subtypes and their therapeutic implications.

title: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, with spontaneous transdural and calvarial invasion: a case report and literature review.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM), IDH-wildtype, is the most aggressive adult-type diffuse glioma. Although extracranial spread may occur after craniotomy, radiotherapy, or other interventions, spontaneous transdural and calvarial invasion before treatment is exceedingly rare. We report a 37-year-old woman who presented with long-standing right temporal-parietal headache and acute worsening with vomiting. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a right temporal mass with intratumoral hemorrhage, peritumoral edema, and contiguous extension through the dura and temporal bone into the temporalis muscle. The lesion was resected through a transcranial approach, and postoperative imaging showed gross total resection. Histological examination demonstrated an infiltrating high-grade glial neoplasm with brisk mitotic activity and palisading necrosis. Immunohistochemical and molecular findings, including the absence of IDH1/IDH2 mutations, supported a diagnosis of glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4. At 18 months after surgery, the patient remained alive. This case highlights a rare pattern of primary extracranial extension in GBM and suggests direct contiguous transdural invasion as a plausible route of spread in the absence of prior intervention.

title: Assessing early therapeutic response in extrapulmonary tuberculosis using [18F]FDG-PET/CT imaging.
abstract: Introduction Monitoring treatment response in extrapulmonary tuberculosis (EPTB) remains challenging due to limited microbiological accessibility and the lack of validated biomarkers. [18F]FDG positron emission tomography/computed tomography [(18F)FDG-PET/CT] enables assessment of metabolic disease activity and has been explored in infectious diseases, but evidence supporting its use in EPTB is limited. Methods We conducted a prospective observational study including adults diagnosed with EPTB at a tertiary referral center in Denmark between 2016 and 2018. Participants underwent baseline and follow-up [18F]FDG-PET/CT imaging after completion of the intensive treatment phase. Clinical data and laboratory parameters, including C-reactive protein (CRP), hemoglobin, leukocytes, albumin, and alanine aminotransferase were collected at baseline and during follow-up. Changes in standardized uptake values (SUVmax) and laboratory markers were analyzed descriptively. Results Seventeen patients were included. Metabolically active disease was detected in all participants at baseline. Most patients (11 out of 14) demonstrated a reduction in lesion number and SUVmax at follow-up, indicating a metabolic response to therapy. However, persistent [18F]FDG uptake was observed in a subset of patients (3 out of 14). Median CRP levels declined from 12 mg/L (range: 0.3-190) at baseline to 3.6 mg/L (range: 0.9-20) at week 8 and remained low thereafter, broadly paralleling PET/CT findings. In several cases, residual metabolic activity did not result in treatment prolongation. Discussion Serial [18F]FDG-PET/CT demonstrated changes in metabolic activity during treatment with reductions in lesion number and SUVmax in most patients. However, SUVmax reflects focal metabolic activity rather than total disease burden, and persistent uptake after the intensive treatment phase was observed in some patients. Larger prospective studies incorporating standardized response criteria and volumetric PET measures are needed before [18F]FDG-PET/CT can be implemented as a routine biomarker for treatment response in EPTB.

title: Artificial intelligence in spinal fracture imaging: from clinical application to translational promise.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping medical imaging, and deep learning together with machine learning are now being used to detect, classify, and differentially diagnose spinal fractures. In this Review, we survey the principal AI architectures that currently support spinal imaging, including convolutional neural networks, object detectors, and hybrid models, and we assess their reported performance for osteoporotic, traumatic, and pathological vertebral fractures. Our synthesis indicates that AI can achieve high diagnostic accuracy in controlled, often single-centre retrospective settings, but its performance consistently declines for mild fractures, degenerated spines, and postoperative anatomy. Critically, the majority of published models lack external validation, and many studies suffer from methodological shortcomings such as selective reporting, insufficient sample sizes, and absence of predefined analysis plans-factors that systematically inflate apparent accuracy. Beyond detection, we explore the growing applications of AI in surgical planning, complication prediction, and functional outcome estimation, while emphasising that most evidence remains preliminary. We identify persistent gaps, including underuse of foundation models and public benchmarks, and limited independent evaluation of commercial tools. We conclude by proposing a shift from performance reporting to methodologically rigorous, prospectively designed studies that incorporate bias assessment, standardised reporting, and patient-centred endpoints-steps essential to translate technical promise into tangible patient benefit.

title: Association of Serum GDF-15 with Bone and Muscle Parameters in Community-Dwelling Individuals.
abstract: Introduction Muscle mass and bone mineral density decrease with aging, although following different patterns among males and females. Growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF-15) is a stress-induced cytokine and has emerged as a key biomarker for inflammation, tissue injury, and metabolic stress. We tested the association between GDF-15 and specific bone and muscle parameters in a large cohort of community-dwelling subjects. Methods The SardiNIA survey included 4,842 subjects (2,795 females). All underwent a detailed medical visit and laboratory testing. Peripheral quantitative computed tomography at the tibia was performed to evaluate volumetric bone mineral density and bone microstructure as well as muscle mass. Results Multivariate regression analysis showed that GDF-15 was negatively associated with cortical bone density (Beta -0.042, p < 0.001) in females. In males, total bone density and trabecular bone density at 4% site and cortical bone area at 38% site were negatively associated with GDF-15 levels (respectively, Beta -0.016, p = 0.027, Beta -0.014, p = 0.039, and Beta -0.022, p = 0.002). Multivariate regression analysis for muscle parameters showed that GDF-15 was negatively associated with muscle density (Beta -0.002 in females and males, p < 0.001 for all) and muscle area (Beta -0.338, p = 0.003, Beta -0.744, p < 0.001). Conclusions Higher circulating GDF-15 levels were independently associated with lower volumetricBMD and poorer muscle parameters in both women and men. These findings support the potential role of GDF-15 as a biomarker of age-related musculoskeletal decline, although longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether GDF-15 contributes to the development of these changes or simply reflects the underlying biological processes.

title: Clinical utility and reproducibility of intravoxel incoherent motion MRI in rectal cancer: a structured narrative review.
abstract: Introduction Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a crucial imaging modality for the management of rectal cancer. Conventional MRI provides detailed anatomical information but has a limited capacity to evaluate tumor biology. Intravoxel Incoherent Motion (IVIM) is an advanced functional MRI technique that simultaneously measures tissue cellularity and microvascular perfusion without contrast agents, providing deeper insights into the tumor microenvironment. This narrative review critically examines the current evidence on the clinical usefulness of IVIM MRI in rectal cancer, focusing on three key areas: tumor characterization and staging, prediction and monitoring of treatment response, and the reproducibility and limitations of IVIM parameters. Methods A literature search was conducted in vid MEDLINE, PubMed, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, and Google Scholar from 2015 to October 2025. The search included keywords such as "intravoxel incoherent motion OR IVIM" and "rectal cancer OR colorectal cancer." Original studies with at least 10 patients were included; reviews, case reports, and animal studies were excluded. title: Intracranial metastasis following intrahepatic remission in primary hepatic small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma: a case report.
abstract: Background Hepatogenic small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (HP-SCNEC) is a highly aggressive rare malignancy, with central nervous system (CNS) metastasis being a major cause of treatment failure. This case report describes a patient with extensively metastatic HP-SCNEC, aiming to explore the clinical features of rapid brain metastasis following complete remission of intrahepatic lesions, as well as corresponding multidisciplinary treatment strategies. Method A retrospective analysis of the diagnostic and therapeutic process in a 60-year-old female patient with HP-SCNEC. At initial presentation, the patient exhibited multiple intrahepatic metastases, abdominal lymph node involvement, and adrenal metastases. First-line therapy comprised the programmed death receptor-1 (PD-1) inhibitor sintilimab combined with etoposide and cisplatin. Following disease progression, whole-brain radiotherapy was administered for newly identified brain metastases, concurrently with systemic treatment adjustment to albumin-bound paclitaxel combined with anlotinib. Results Following 6 cycles of immunotherapy combined with chemotherapy and 2 cycles of immunotherapy combined with anti-angiogenic therapy, the patient achieved radiographic complete remission of hepatic lesions. However, merely 16 days after achieving this remission, the patient presented with new-onset neurological symptoms, and subsequent imaging confirmed multiple new brain metastases. After undergoing whole-brain radiotherapy combined with an adjusted systemic treatment regimen, intracranial lesions were effectively controlled. The patient remained stable during subsequent maintenance therapy with Anlotinib. Conclusion This case demonstrates that even when HP-SCNEC abdominal lesions achieve deep remission through intensified immunotherapy combined with chemotherapy, patients remain at extremely high risk for early brain metastases, highlighting the "intracranial sanctuary" effect caused by the blood-brain barrier. For such patients, prevention and monitoring of central nervous system metastases must be prioritized during initial treatment. Following brain metastasis, a multimodal comprehensive strategy centered on radiotherapy combined with intracranial active drugs should be adopted. This case provides important reference for the comprehensive management of this rare malignant tumor.

title: Dual-phase CTA filling pattern is associated with reperfusion-related complications after mechanical thrombectomy in late-window anterior circulation stroke.
abstract: Objective To evaluate whether pre-treatment dual-phase computed tomography angiography (CTA) filling patterns are independently associated with reperfusion-related complications after late-window mechanical thrombectomy and whether they provide incremental prognostic value beyond conventional clinical and imaging variables. Methods We conducted a prospective single-center cohort study including 80 consecutive patients with anterior circulation large-vessel occlusion who underwent mechanical thrombectomy within 6-24 h after stroke onset or last known well. Dual-phase CTA filling patterns were classified as good early filling, delayed filling, or persistent poor filling; delayed and persistent poor filling were combined for the primary analyses. The primary outcome was a composite of reperfusion-related complications within 72 h, including hemorrhagic transformation ≥HI2, malignant cerebral edema, or early neurological deterioration. Secondary outcomes were 90-day functional independence and all-cause mortality. Independent predictors were identified using Firth penalized logistic regression. Incremental model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis, bootstrap internal validation, reclassification metrics, and decision-curve analysis. Results Reperfusion-related complications occurred in 28 patients (35%) and were significantly more frequent in patients with delayed or poor filling than in those with good early filling (56% vs. 20%; p < 0.001). Delayed or poor filling independently predicted reperfusion-related complications after adjustment for age, baseline NIHSS score, and ASPECTS (adjusted OR 3.97, 95% CI 1.22-14.10; p = 0.022). Older age was also independently associated with increased risk (adjusted OR 2.14 per 10-year increase, 95% CI 1.24-4.12; p = 0.005), whereas higher ASPECTS was protective (adjusted OR 0.35 per point, 95% CI 0.18-0.61; p < 0.001). The full model incorporating dual-phase CTA achieved excellent discrimination (AUC 0.895; optimism-corrected AUC 0.867). Addition of the dual-phase CTA filling pattern improved patient risk reclassification, although the increase in discrimination beyond the clinical-plus-ASPECTS model was not statistically significant. Patients with delayed or poor filling had substantially worse 90-day outcomes, including lower functional independence (24% vs. 70%) and higher mortality (38% vs. 4%) (both p < 0.001). Conclusions Delayed or persistent poor filling on dual-phase CTA is an independent imaging marker of reperfusion-related complications following late-window mechanical thrombectomy. Although its incremental contribution to model discrimination was modest, dual-phase CTA may improve early risk stratification and help identify patients who may benefit from intensified post-procedural monitoring. External validation is warranted before routine clinical implementation.

title: AI-driven CT assessment of erector spinae myosteatosis: muscle quality and its association with strength and frailty in older surgical patients.
abstract: Background Frailty and sarcopenia are overlapping syndromes that increase adverse outcomes in older adults. Computed tomography (CT) is a reference standard for body composition analysis, but manual segmentation is time-consuming. This exploratory study used a fully automated deep learning model (DLM) to investigate associations between CT-derived muscle quality and quantity and clinical frailty. Methods We performed a retrospective, cross-sectional secondary analysis of 53 geriatric surgical patients (mean age 77.4 ± 4.4 years). A DLM segmented skeletal muscle (SM), subcutaneous and visceral adipose tissue at the third lumbar vertebral level. Intermuscular adipose tissue (IMAT) was quantified exclusively within the erector spinae muscle and is therefore reported as a surrogate marker of trunk muscle quality rather than whole-muscle myosteatosis. Frailty was assessed with the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS), handgrip strength and the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test. Because functional testing was incomplete, effective sample sizes varied ( n = 21-53) and are reported for every model. Results In the total cohort, a higher IMAT Index was associated with lower handgrip strength ( ρ = -0.434, p = 0.004, n = 43) and remained independent after adjustment for age, sex, BMI and ASA status (B = -1.808, 95% CI -2.994 to -0.622, p = 0.004, n = 42). Its association with the CFS was borderline univariately ( ρ = 0.273, p = 0.051, n = 52) and absent after adjustment ( p = 0.184, n = 51). Neither index was independently associated with TUG performance ( p = 0.134 and p = 0.071, n = 25). In an exploratory sex-stratified analysis, the IMAT Index correlated with the CFS in women ( ρ = 0.727, p < 0.001, n = 19) but not in men. Because the female subgroup was small ( n = 20), no sex-stratified regression or interaction test was performed. Conclusions In this small, retrospective, cross-sectional cohort, an erector-spinae-based IMAT Index was associated with handgrip strength but not independently with global clinical frailty. Automated opportunistic CT analysis may therefore identify specific muscle weakness rather than global frailty. The observed sex differences are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger, adequately powered longitudinal studies.

title: Case Report: Synchronous double primary male breast cancer and non-small cell lung cancer: diagnostic confirmation and multidisciplinary management.
abstract: Background Male breast cancer (MBC) is rare, accounting for approximately 1% of all breast cancers. When MBC is diagnosed simultaneously with a second primary lung cancer, treatment planning becomes particularly complex because diagnostic certainty, technical resectability, competing treatment windows, and radiotherapy safety must all be considered. Case presentation We report a 72-year-old man who was synchronously diagnosed with left invasive ductal breast carcinoma and right lower lobe poorly differentiated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The breast cancer was staged as pT 3 N 2a M 0 , AJCC 8th edition stage IIIA, with strong ER/PR expression and HER2 nonamplification. The lung lesion was pathologically diagnosed as poorly differentiated NSCLC without definitive glandular, squamous, or neuroendocrine differentiation and was staged as cT 3 N 0 M 0 , AJCC 8th edition stage IIB. Although stage IIB NSCLC is usually evaluated for surgery, this tumor closely involved the right lower lobe pulmonary vessels and bronchial structures, and thoracic surgeons considered upfront radical resection technically unsafe because of the risks of hemorrhage, extended resection, impaired blood supply to the remaining lobes, and loss of pulmonary function. After multidisciplinary team (MDT) discussion, the patient underwent left modified radical mastectomy, adjuvant AC-T chemotherapy, and simultaneous postmastectomy radiotherapy to the left chest wall/regional nodes with definitive radiotherapy to the right lung lesion plus concurrent cisplatin. Imaging shortly after radiotherapy showed marked shrinkage of the right lung lesion, but subsequent CT and liver MRI suggested systemic progression with multiple hepatic lesions. The patient declined liver biopsy, received one cycle of vinorelbine plus cisplatin with Endostar, discontinued further treatment, and died of liver failure in March 2026. Conclusion This case illustrates that therapeutic prioritization in synchronous double primary cancers should not be determined solely by TNM stage or chronological order of diagnosis. Instead, treatment decisions should integrate pathological distinction, tumor biology, anatomical treatability, technical resectability, curative potential, competing treatment windows, and short-term clinical threat. In selected patients, simultaneous postmastectomy radiotherapy and definitive lung radiotherapy may be feasible when supported by MDT consensus, dosimetric review, and close toxicity monitoring.

title: Reconstruction-aware radiomics for risk stratification of subsolid pulmonary nodules: technical evidence, clinical limits, and translation priorities.
abstract: Subsolid pulmonary nodules (SSNs), including pure ground-glass nodules (pGGNs) and part-solid nodules (PSNs), span transient inflammatory abnormalities and adenocarcinoma-spectrum lesions with widely different management implications. This critical narrative review treats CT reconstruction as part of the quantitative biomarker definition and asks whether targeted or high-spatial-resolution reconstruction provides stable, task-specific information beyond standardized thin-section CT. Evidence was synthesized across direct SSN reconstruction-domain studies, technical robustness studies, and clinical prediction studies. Direct imaging studies support improved depiction of selected fine structures, while same-scan GGN evidence demonstrates substantial pixel-size dependence of radiomic features and model composition. However, most clinical models were not evaluated in paired reconstruction domains, external validation with calibration remains uncommon, and no prospective study demonstrating management or patient benefit from reconstruction-aware radiomics in SSNs was identified in the literature reviewed. Persistent pGGNs provide a biological and technical rationale for investigating incremental quantitative information, but greater benefit than in PSNs has not been demonstrated. In PSNs, any model must add value beyond solid-component measurements, consolidation-to-tumor ratio, morphology, and longitudinal growth. Translation therefore requires reconstruction and segmentation robustness testing, strong conventional comparators, external calibration, prespecified thresholds, and prospective decision-linked evaluation. Until such benefit and safety are demonstrated, reconstruction-aware radiomics should remain investigational or confined to governed, domain-checked decision-support pathways.

title: FroHyNet: frozen temporal priors and trainable hypergraph fusion for brain time-series classification.
abstract: Background Functional brain time-series classification is constrained by small clinical cohorts. Handcrafted features are sample-efficient but discard temporal detail; end-to-end networks must estimate many temporal parameters from limited labels; and frozen time-series foundation models reduce that estimation burden but typically encode each channel independently, leaving coordinated activity across brain regions unmodeled. Methods We introduce the Frozen Temporal-Hypergraph Network (FroHyNet), an asymmetric parallel framework that preserves channel-wise temporal representations from a frozen MantisV2 encoder while a trainable spatio-temporal hypergraph branch learns topology-aware spatial corrections. Bottleneck-mix Top-K (BM-TopK) then residual-injects these corrections only along selected channel and latent-feature axes, treating the spatial stream as a selective update rather than a dense overwrite of the temporal representation. We conduct five-fold cross-validation across two functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and three functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets. Results FroHyNet achieves the best average accuracy and area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUC) among methods evaluated on all five datasets, while keeping the trainable-parameter count well below those of from-scratch temporal networks. Gains are concentrated on fNIRS, with more modest improvements on the smaller fMRI cohorts. Branch ablations indicate dataset-dependent complementarity between the two streams, and fusion ablations on HC-D favor BM-TopK over the evaluated dense and recurrent alternatives.

title: Concurrent Bartholin gland and perianal abscesses in a woman: a case report of a diagnostic challenge.
abstract: Background Bartholin gland abscess and perianal abscess are common suppurative infections involving anatomically adjacent regions of the female perineum. Because both conditions may present with localized pain and swelling, distinguishing their respective origins and determining the extent of infection can be challenging. The concomitant occurrence of these two abscesses is uncommon, and its diagnostic and therapeutic considerations remain poorly characterized. We report a rare case of concomitant Bartholin gland and perianal abscesses and describe the diagnostic process and multidisciplinary surgical management. Case presentation An 18-year-old woman presented with progressive perineal and perianal pain and swelling. Pelvic computed tomography demonstrated abscess formation involving the perianal and left perineal soft tissues, and a possible communication between the two lesions was initially suspected. Emergency surgery was performed. The perianal abscess was incised and drained, and an infected anal gland was identified and excised, with bridge drainage established between the drainage incisions. Intraoperative exploration revealed no communication between the perianal abscess and the adjacent perineal lesion. Following gynecological consultation, the separate left vulvar abscess was drained and treated with Jacobi ring fistulization. Culture of the perineal abscess grew Escherichia coli, whereas the perianal abscess culture showed no bacterial growth. Follow-up magnetic resonance imaging 1 month after surgery demonstrated a cystic lesion in the anatomical region of the left Bartholin gland, supporting the Bartholin gland origin of the previously drained perineal abscess. The patient showed satisfactory clinical recovery, with complete healing of the perianal and perineal wounds at 4 months and no evidence of recurrent abscess during the available follow-up. Conclusion Concomitant Bartholin gland and perianal abscesses may be difficult to distinguish because of their overlapping clinical manifestations and anatomical proximity. Clinicians should consider the possibility of multiple independent or potentially related infectious foci and systematically evaluate adjacent anatomical regions. Careful physical examination, appropriate imaging, intraoperative assessment, and timely multidisciplinary collaboration can facilitate accurate diagnosis and individualized surgical management.

title: Case Report: Distal ureteral obstruction decades after presumed intrauterine device removal in a woman with uterus didelphys.
abstract: Background An ectopic intrauterine device (IUD) can rarely cause ureteral obstruction and hydroureteronephrosis. Diagnosis may be delayed when a prior removal procedure is believed to have been complete. Case presentation A 48-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of right flank pain and urinary frequency after repeated treatment for presumed urinary tract infection and possible genitourinary tuberculosis without sustained improvement. More than 20 years earlier, an IUD had been inserted before uterus didelphys was recognized. Two to three years later, an unintended pregnancy led to recognition of the duplicated uterine anatomy, induced abortion, and an IUD removal procedure. The original records were unavailable, so device location and intact retrieval at that time could not be verified. Multimodality imaging at the index admission showed severe right hydroureteronephrosis, focal distal ureteral narrowing, and an ectopic metallic IUD outside both uterine cavities; cystoscopy was unremarkable. Open ureteral exploration and reconstruction identified an intact IUD with an attached calculus externally compressing an approximately 1-cm fixed distal ureteral stricture without entering the ureteral lumen. The narrowing persisted after device removal, requiring segmental ureteral resection and anastomosis over a double-J stent. Histopathology of the resected ureter showed chronic inflammatory changes without tuberculous changes. The stent was removed 2 months postoperatively. At 6 months after surgery, computed tomography showed marked decompression of the right collecting system and no residual pelvic metallic device; serum creatinine remained normal. Conclusion A history of IUD removal should not be treated as proof of device absence when intact retrieval is undocumented. In otherwise unexplained unilateral ureteral obstruction, a remote IUD history should prompt review of prior device localization and targeted pelvic imaging, particularly when historical records are unavailable or duplicated uterine anatomy complicates localization. A fixed stricture may require reconstruction even after the ectopic device is removed.

title: Case Report: Durable, well-tolerated complete response to epcoritamab plus pirtobrutinib in Richter transformation relapsing after CD19 CAR T-cell therapy.
abstract: Richter transformation (RT) that relapses after CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has no established therapy and carries a dismal prognosis. We report an 84-year-old man with multiply relapsed, biopsy-proven diffuse large B-cell lymphoma-type RT and a high-risk MYC/BCL2 double-expressor phenotype who developed systemic relapse, with extensive osteolytic bone disease, after lisocabtagene maraleucel. Three cycles of atezolizumab produced no objective benefit. Treatment with epcoritamab, a CD3xCD20 bispecific antibody, plus pirtobrutinib, a non-covalent Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor, produced complete nodal metabolic resolution within 3 months that deepened to a complete metabolic response (Deauville score 2) by 10 treatment cycles, with resolution of two interim osteolytic lesions whose transient nature illustrates the interpretive challenges of PET/CT response assessment after cellular and T-cell-engaging therapies. The chemotherapy-free regimen was well tolerated at age 84, with no cytokine release syndrome, no neurotoxicity, and no cytopenias; the only toxicity was mild, reversible dexamethasone-related myopathy. The patient remains in ongoing clinical remission after approximately 10 months of therapy. This case extends the reported experience with epcoritamab plus pirtobrutinib specifically to the post-CAR T-cell relapse setting and suggests that this chemotherapy-free doublet may warrant consideration as a salvage strategy for older or frail patients with RT who are unfit for further cytotoxic therapy.

title: Serum GDF15 as a potential biomarker for treatment response and survival in patients with resectable locally advanced gastric cancer undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
abstract: Background Patients with locally advanced gastric cancer (LAGC) typically require neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) to reduce tumor burden and improve surgical resectability. However, treatment responses to NAC vary substantially among individuals. This study investigated the potential value of baseline serum growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) for identifying patients at risk of poor treatment response and unfavorable survival outcomes among patients with LAGC receiving NAC. Methods We retrospectively identified 318 eligible patients with LAGC who received NAC and enrolled 30 healthy controls. Serum GDF15 levels were measured by ELISA. In the unmatched cohort, the median baseline serum GDF15 concentration (2,147.3 pg/mL), determined before PSM, was used as a fixed cutoff to define the GDF15-L and GDF15-H groups (n = 159 each). After 1:1 PSM, 256 patients (n = 128 per group) were included in the matched analyses. Comparative analyses included baseline characteristics, CT images, preoperative endoscopic biopsy specimens and postoperative pathological features. Survival outcomes (OS and DFS) were assessed via Kaplan-Meier analysis. Multivariate Cox regression identified prognostic factors, and a prognostic nomogram was constructed. Results High GDF15 expression correlated with advanced age (P = 0.045), poor tumor differentiation (P = 0.040), and elevated serum CA72-4 (P = 0.028). The GDF15-L group demonstrated superior median OS (58.1 vs. 54.0 months, P = 0.031) and DFS (47.1 vs. 26.9 months, P = 0.002) compared to GDF15-H counterparts. Preoperative endoscopic biopsy demonstrated a positive correlation between tissue GDF15 expression and serum GDF15 levels, while post-NAC imaging indicated greater tumor regression in the GDF15-L group. The GDF15-L group exhibited a higher pathological complete response (pCR) rate in postoperative pathological features (P < 0.001) while the GDF15-H group exhibited increased positive lymph nodes (P = 0.018) and a higher incidence of newly detected distant metastasis during or after NAC (P = 0.024). Multivariate analysis identified high GDF15 expression (P = 0.021) and high CAP degree (P = 0.022) as independent risk factors for OS, with younger age being protective (P = 0.016). Based on these factors, a prognostic nomogram was constructed to predict 1-year, 3-year, and 5-year OS and DFS. Conclusion Low baseline serum GDF15 levels were associated with favorable radiological and pathological responses and prolonged survival in patients with LAGC receiving NAC. Baseline serum GDF15 may help identify patients at increased risk of poor response and unfavorable prognosis and may therefore serve as a potential biomarker for pretreatment risk stratification. However, because all patients received NAC, these findings do not establish that GDF15 predicts differential benefit from NAC, and prospective validation is required.

title: The role of vascular pathology in SMA: implications for pathogenesis and treatment.
abstract: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) has become a paradigm for precision medicine following the development of transformative therapies targeting the disease-causing deficiency of survival motor neuron (SMN) protein. As more than 98% of SMA cases arise from mutations in the SMN1 gene, restoration of SMN expression through nusinersen (Spinraza; Biogen, Cambridge, MA), risdiplam (Evrysdi; Roche, Basel, Switzerland) and onasemnogene abeparvovec (Zolgensma and Itvisma; AveXis, Novartis, Chicago, IL) has produced unprecedented clinical benefits and established SMA as the first treatable motor neuron disease. To date, therapeutic success has focused on rescuing motor neurons, the principal site of clinical pathology. However, growing evidence indicates that SMA is a multisystem disorder in which pathological changes extend beyond the motor unit. In particular, vascular pathology has emerged as a recurring feature across numerous affected tissues. Vascular abnormalities have been identified throughout the neuromuscular system, including the spinal cord and skeletal muscle, as well as in systemic organs such as the heart, kidney, gastrointestinal tract and spleen. Experimental studies suggest that endothelial dysfunction is a direct consequence of SMN deficiency, impairing angiogenesis, vascular maturation and vessel stability, while patient-derived biomarkers, including retinal vascular imaging and elevated circulating endothelial cells (CEC), provide evidence of ongoing endothelial dysfunction in patients. These vascular abnormalities have the potential to compromise tissue perfusion, promote local hypoxia, disrupt barrier integrity and enhance inflammatory signaling, thereby exacerbating disease progression. Collectively, the evidence suggests that SMN-dependent vascular pathology may represent an under-recognized feature of SMA pathogenesis and a potential therapeutic target. Here, we review the current evidence for vascular pathology in SMA, discuss its implications for disease progression, long-term patient outcomes and therapeutic response, and consider whether vascular abnormalities are adequately addressed by existing SMN-restorative therapies.

title: MEMOIR-VLM-a multimodal vision-language model for Alzheimer's disease classification and question answering.
abstract: Introduction Alzheimer's disease (AD) affects an estimated 55 million people worldwide and is projected to nearly double by 2050, creating a need for scalable, non-invasive AI systems that can classify disease stage, support multimodal clinical reasoning, and interact in natural language. Most deep learning work on AD focuses on single-modality classification without natural-language interaction and typically assumes complete input data. Methods We present MEMOIR-VLM (Multimodal Encoder with Missing-modality and Open-ended Inference for Retrieval), a modular two-stage vision-language framework trained and evaluated on 2,363 ADNI subjects. The first stage is a missing-modality-aware encoder that fuses T1-weighted MRI and DTI fractional anisotropy maps with structured clinical scores via cross-attention fusion with stochastic modality dropout, allowing a single set of weights to operate on any of the seven non-empty modality subsets without imputation. After CLIP/InfoNCE contrastive pretraining, the encoder is fine-tuned for multi-task prediction of 3-way diagnosis, binary diagnosis, CDR-SB, age, and sex. The second stage extends the frozen encoder into a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline for case-based reasoning and open-ended visual question answering. Results On held-out ADNI test data, with CDR-SB excluded from the inputs to remove a cognitive-score leak, the encoder achieved 91.3% balanced accuracy for CN vs. dementia and 68.2% balanced accuracy for 3-class diagnosis (macro-F1 = 0.681); age was predicted with a 5.96-year MAE. When the diagnosis field was withheld from retrieved captions, no evaluated LLM exceeded a retrieval-only k-NN majority vote (0.673), which itself closely matched the encoder's 3-class accuracy (0.682). The RAG-VQA layer showed strong text fidelity (BERTScore = 0.894; SBERT cosine similarity = 0.811). Zero-shot external validation on OASIS-3 (1,048 subjects, no diffusion data) retained 78.7% balanced accuracy for CN vs. impaired (AUC = 0.889) using identical ADNI-trained weights with the DTI branch masked. Discussion MEMOIR-VLM combines missing-modality-aware multimodal encoding, multi-task clinical prediction, and retrieval-grounded natural-language reasoning within a single modular framework. The results support using the encoder, optionally with k-NN voting, as the diagnostic component and the RAG-VQA layer as an interpretable natural-language interface that surfaces comparable cases and readable clinical summaries. The external validation results further demonstrate the practical value of the missing-modality mechanism when an imaging modality is unavailable.

After CLIP/InfoNCE contrastive pretraining, the encoder is fine-tuned for multi-task prediction of 3-way diagnosis, binary diagnosis, CDR-SB, age, and sex. The second stage extends the frozen encoder into a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline for case-based reasoning and open-ended visual question answering.

Results

On held-out ADNI test data, with CDR-SB excluded from the inputs to remove a cognitive-score leak, the encoder achieved 91.3% balanced accuracy for CN vs. dementia and 68.2% balanced accuracy for 3-class diagnosis (macro-F1 = 0.681); age was predicted with a 5.96-year MAE. When the diagnosis field was withheld from retrieved captions, no evaluated LLM exceeded a retrieval-only k-NN majority vote (0.673), which itself closely matched the encoder's 3-class accuracy (0.682). The RAG-VQA layer showed strong text fidelity (BERTScore = 0.894; SBERT cosine similarity = 0.811). Zero-shot external validation on OASIS-3 (1,048 subjects, no diffusion data) retained 78.7% balanced accuracy for CN vs. impaired (AUC = 0.889) using identical ADNI-trained weights with the DTI branch masked.

Discussion

MEMOIR-VLM combines missing-modality-aware multimodal encoding, multi-task clinical prediction, and retrieval-grounded natural-language reasoning within a single modular framework. The results support using the encoder, optionally with k-NN voting, as the diagnostic component and the RAG-VQA layer as an interpretable natural-language interface that surfaces comparable cases and readable clinical summaries. The external validation results further demonstrate the practical value of the missing-modality mechanism when an imaging modality is unavailable.

title: Neuromelanin-sensitive magnetic resonance imaging in the diagnosis and assessment of Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized primarily by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc); noradrenergic neurons in the locus coeruleus (LC) are also frequently affected. Because clinical motor symptoms usually emerge only after substantial neurodegeneration has occurred, there is a compelling need for noninvasive imaging biomarkers capable of detecting early pathological changes. Neuromelanin-sensitive magnetic resonance imaging (NM-MRI) generates neuromelanin-related image contrast in the SNpc and LC and can indirectly reflect the structural integrity of these catecholaminergic nuclei. Current evidence suggests that NM-MRI may be useful for distinguishing patients with PD from healthy controls, supporting the differential diagnosis of selected atypical parkinsonian syndromes and essential tremor, assessing disease stage, monitoring longitudinal change, and evaluating high-risk individuals in the prodromal phase. This review provides an updated account of recent advances in the use of NM-MRI for diagnostic support, differential diagnosis, prodromal assessment, longitudinal monitoring, multimodal imaging, and artificial intelligence-based analysis, and discusses its clinical role relative to other imaging and fluid biomarkers. Combining NM-MRI with complementary imaging measures, such as quantitative susceptibility mapping and diffusion MRI, and with automated analytical methods may further enhance pathological characterization and quantitative assessment. However, the available evidence is derived largely from single-center or case-control studies with limited sample sizes. Substantial variability may arise from differences in scanners, magnetic field strengths, acquisition protocols, and analytical methods, while independent external validation and prospective multicenter longitudinal evidence remain limited. The biological basis of the NM-MRI signal has not been fully established, and artificial intelligence models developed for NM-MRI remain vulnerable to overfitting, limited interpretability, and limited cross-center generalizability. Accordingly, NM-MRI cannot currently serve as a stand-alone diagnostic tool for PD or replace diagnosis based on comprehensive clinical assessment. It is better regarded as a promising complementary imaging biomarker and research tool. Before NM-MRI can be widely used for routine clinical diagnosis, disease monitoring, or as a clinical trial outcome measure, acquisition and analytical methods must be further standardized, and its performance must be evaluated in large, prospective, multicenter longitudinal studies.

title: Admission TRIAGES score for unfavorable functional outcome after traumatic brain injury: association, prognostic performance, and comparison with the Glasgow coma scale.
abstract: Background The Trauma Rating Index in Age, Glasgow Coma Scale, Respiratory rate, and Systolic blood pressure (TRIAGES) is a simple trauma score that has shown prognostic value for short-term mortality in traumatic brain injury (TBI), but its relationship with functional outcome remains insufficiently characterized. Methods We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study of adults with TBI admitted between June 2017 and May 2026. The primary exposure was the TRIAGES score calculated using age and the first GCS, respiratory rate, and systolic blood pressure values recorded at initial emergency department presentation before any in-hospital therapeutic intervention. Admission GCS was defined as the GCS value obtained at this same initial assessment. The primary outcome was unfavorable functional status at hospital discharge, defined as a discharge Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS) score of 1-3. Multivariable logistic regression, restricted cubic spline analysis, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, calibration, Brier score, decision curve analysis, bootstrap internal validation, sensitivity analyses, and subgroup analyses were performed. Results Among 753 patients, 181 (24.0%) had an unfavorable functional outcome. Each 1-point increase in TRIAGES was independently associated with higher odds of unfavorable functional status after adjustment for sex, injury mechanism, number of non-reactive pupils, and Rotterdam CT score (adjusted odds ratio 2.81, 95% confidence interval 2.29-3.45; p < 0.001). The association was approximately linear (P for non-linearity = 0.366). TRIAGES alone achieved an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.905 compared with 0.890 for admission GCS alone (ΔAUC = 0.015, 95% CI 0.001-0.029; paired DeLong p = 0.034). Within this cohort, a Youden index-derived threshold of TRIAGES ≥3 yielded a sensitivity of 0.956 and specificity of 0.701. Bootstrap internal validation showed an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.905, and the findings remained consistent across multiple sensitivity analyses. Conclusion Higher TRIAGES scores at initial emergency presentation were independently associated with unfavorable functional status at hospital discharge in adults with TBI. TRIAGES showed good prognostic performance and a small within-cohort increase in discrimination relative to admission GCS alone while retaining the practical advantage of using only four routinely available variables. Prospective multicenter studies with external validation and standardized long-term functional outcomes are warranted.

title: Deep brain stimulation and spinal cord stimulation for chronic disorders of consciousness: a decade of clinical evidence, mechanistic insights, and critical appraisal.
abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) and spinal cord stimulation (SCS) have been investigated for over four decades as neuromodulatory treatments for chronic disorders of consciousness (DOC), including the vegetative state/unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (VS/UWS) and the minimally conscious state (MCS), for which no disease-modifying pharmacological therapy exists. This narrative review synthesizes literature published between 2016 and 2026 on the neurobiological rationale, clinical evidence, neurophysiological biomarkers, and safety of DBS and SCS for chronic DOC. The 'mesocircuit hypothesis', supported by human intraoperative electrophysiology and nonhuman primate causal manipulation, provides a coherent rationale for central thalamic and centromedian-parafascicular targeting. Across case series, cohort studies, and individual patient data meta-analyses, both DBS and SCS produce clinically meaningful improvement in a minority of patients, consistently more often in MCS (63-74% response) than in VS/UWS (26-30% response), with younger age and shorter injury-to-treatment interval predicting better outcomes. However, the two largest individual patient data meta-analyses of DBS concur that current evidence is insufficient to conclude that stimulation alters the natural history of neurological recovery beyond what would be expected from patient selection and spontaneous recovery, and adverse event rates (8.1% for SCS, 18.2% for DBS) indicate non-trivial surgical risk in this vulnerable population. Neurophysiological and neuroimaging biomarkers derived from EEG, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, functional MRI, and FDG-PET show promise for objective outcome prediction but await prospective validation. We conclude that DBS and SCS remain experimental, mechanistically motivated but not yet definitively proven therapies for chronic DOC, and that adequately powered randomized controlled trials, biomarker-guided patient selection, and dedicated ethical frameworks are needed before either modality can be recommended outside of research settings.

title: Transformers for fMRI analysis: from spatiotemporal modeling to brain foundation models.
abstract: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) serves as a pivotal tool for investigating the functional organization and dynamic connectivity of the human brain, indirectly reflecting neural activity through blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signals. However, the high-dimensional spatiotemporal structure, prominent noise interference, and inter-individual variability of fMRI data pose significant challenges for traditional modeling methods in characterizing complex brain functional patterns. In recent years, the Transformer architecture has gained significant traction in fMRI data analysis, leveraging its self-attention mechanism to model global dependencies. It has demonstrated superior performance in tasks such as brain disease classification, functional connectivity modeling, and brain representation learning. Compared to convolutional and recurrent neural networks, Transformers can more effectively capture long-range spatiotemporal dependencies and offer stronger structural scalability and cross-task transfer potential. To systematically map the development of this field, this paper proposes a unified taxonomy for Transformer-fMRI methods based on modeling dimensions. It categorizes existing research into four primary paradigms: temporal modeling, spatial modeling, spatiotemporal joint modeling, and self-supervised learning, providing a comparative analysis of their structural characteristics and applicable scenarios. Furthermore, this paper summarizes the key challenges regarding computational complexity, data dependency, and interpretability, while exploring the integration of neuroscientific priors with large-scale pre-trained models. Finally, we discuss future directions for Transformers in the construction of brain foundation models and their clinical utility.

title: Cortical surface morphometry changes following combined translingual neural stimulation with the portable neuromodulation stimulator and physical therapy in patients with mild-to-moderate traumatic brain injury: a pilot study.
abstract: Background Traumatic brain injury (TBI) often causes persistent balance and gait deficits, especially in mild-to-moderate TBI (mmTBI). Physical therapy is standard but often limited as a standalone treatment. Translingual neural stimulation (TLNS) is an emerging neuromodulation approach combining cranial nerve stimulation with targeted exercise to promote neuroplasticity and recovery. Its effects on cortical surface morphometry in mmTBI remain uninvestigated. Methods This secondary analysis used data from a completed clinical trial (NCT02158494). Nine chronic mmTBI patients underwent a two-week intervention combining TLNS (PoNS®) with targeted exercise training; no untreated, physical-therapy-only, or sham group was included. Balance and gait were assessed via the Sensory Organization Test (SOT) and Dynamic Gait Index (DGI) before and after the two-week in-lab phase. High-resolution T1-weighted MRI was acquired at both time points. Cortical thickness (CT), fractal dimensionality (FD), gyrification index (GI), and sulcal depth (SD) were analyzed using CAT12 with non-parametric permutation testing and TFCE correction. Results SOT and DGI scores improved significantly; due to the single-group design, these pre-post changes cannot be attributed to TLNS, physical therapy, or their combination. Widespread pre-post CT increases occurred in bilateral frontal, temporal, parietal, and cingulate regions. FD showed increases (precuneus, insula, and superior frontal gyrus) and decreases (lateral occipital, inferior temporal gyri). GI decreased in the left lingual gyrus; SD showed bidirectional changes. Exploratory correlations linked greater behavioral gains with smaller CT increases in right inferior temporal gyrus and right superior parietal lobule, and smaller FD increases in left precuneus; these were underpowered ( N = 9), uncorrected, and hypothesis-generating only. Morphometric changes in either direction cannot be assumed to reflect beneficial neuroplasticity. Conclusion In this exploratory, single-group pilot study, cortical surface morphometric changes accompanied balance and gait improvements after combined TLNS plus physical therapy in mm TBI. Without a control group, causality cannot be determined. Findings are preliminary and support randomized, sham-controlled trials, ideally with a physical-therapy-only arm.

title: From task-specific AI to multimodal foundation models in PET/CT: a readiness framework for clinical translation.
abstract: Artificial intelligence in PET/CT is evolving from narrowly optimized systems toward reusable pretrained representations and multimodal models. PET/CT is a demanding test case because clinically meaningful interpretation must preserve quantitative molecular information while integrating anatomic CT, acquisition metadata, longitudinal examinations, and free-text imaging reports. This focused narrative review synthesizes literature reported from January 2021 through July 2026, spanning PET reconstruction and enhancement, attenuation correction, segmentation, outcome modeling, pretrained representations, vision-language systems, and agentic workflows. We distinguish task-specific models, reusable pretrained representations, promptable models, vision-language systems, generalist foundation-model candidates, and agentic systems according to demonstrated capabilities, while separately considering evaluation benchmarks. Task-specific deep learning has demonstrated promising technical performance in low-count imaging and whole-body tumor analysis, but most evidence remains retrospective and restricted by radiotracer, disease, scanner, institution, or endpoint. Emerging PET-native studies demonstrate label-efficient segmentation, image-text grounding, report generation, and modular tool orchestration; however, they do not yet establish broad cross-tracer generalization or prospective clinical benefit. We therefore propose MOSAIC-PET, an author-developed heuristic six-domain evaluation framework for PET/CT foundation models encompassing Molecular fidelity, Organ and anatomic grounding, Semantic faithfulness, Adaptability, Integration and clinical impact, and Continuous governance. MOSAIC-PET has not undergone Delphi consensus or formal validation and is intended to organize PET-specific evidence requirements rather than function as a validated clinical-readiness tool. The near-term translational priority is the development of modular, auditable systems in which validated quantitative tools and evidence-linked language outputs remain under specialist oversight, with progression from external testing to silent evaluation, assisted-use studies, clinical-impact assessment, and continuous lifecycle monitoring.

Emerging PET-native studies demonstrate label-efficient segmentation, image-text grounding, report generation, and modular tool orchestration; however, they do not yet establish broad cross-tracer generalization or prospective clinical benefit. We therefore propose MOSAIC-PET, an author-developed heuristic six-domain evaluation framework for PET/CT foundation models encompassing Molecular fidelity, Organ and anatomic grounding, Semantic faithfulness, Adaptability, Integration and clinical impact, and Continuous governance. MOSAIC-PET has not undergone Delphi consensus or formal validation and is intended to organize PET-specific evidence requirements rather than function as a validated clinical-readiness tool. The near-term translational priority is the development of modular, auditable systems in which validated quantitative tools and evidence-linked language outputs remain under specialist oversight, with progression from external testing to silent evaluation, assisted-use studies, clinical-impact assessment, and continuous lifecycle monitoring.

title: Predictive value of multimodal models combining CT body composition and clinical variables for short-term postoperative complications in colorectal cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background Malnutrition and sarcopenic obesity are prevalent in colorectal cancer (CRC) and linked to adverse surgical outcomes. Conventional screening often overlooks this occult malnutrition. Preoperative computed tomography (CT)-based body composition analysis (BCA) provides objective biomarkers for muscle depletion and fat distribution. This systematic review evaluates multimodal machine learning (ML) models integrating BCA and clinical variables to predict CRC postoperative complications and inform precision nutrition strategies. Methods We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library (inception to April 13, 2026) for ML models predicting postoperative complications in CRC using BCA. Quality was assessed using PROBAST. Pooled area under the curve (AUC) was estimated via a random-effects model, alongside subgroup analyses. Results Eight studies ( n = 7,835) were included. The pooled AUC was 0.84 (95% CI: 0.76-0.89), indicating good discriminative performance, although substantial heterogeneity was present ( I 2 = 79.7%). Nomogram-based models showed a pooled AUC of 0.87 (95% CI: 0.78-0.92). For anastomotic leakage, the pooled AUC was 0.83 (95% CI: 0.35-0.98), although this estimate was imprecise because only two studies contributed to this subgroup. Conclusion Multimodal ML models integrating BCA biomarkers offer a robust, data-driven framework for preoperative risk stratification in CRC. Identifying high-risk body composition phenotypes may facilitate tailored prehabilitation and targeted immunonutrition strategies. Future efforts must prioritize standardized BCA and multi-center external validation. Systematic review registration CRD420261364363.

title: Genetic risk stratification reveals distinct first-order radiomic phenotypes in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Background Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) exhibits significant morphological heterogeneity that has traditionally been attributed to etiological, environmental, and biological factors. Recent evidence suggests, however, that genetic background may influence tumor characteristics and behavior in HCC. Purpose To investigate associations between established HCC genetic risk factors and first-order radiomic features. Methods We evaluated a retrospective cohort of 210 patients with HCC who underwent contrast-enhanced MRI and genetic profiling for three established HCC risk variants (PNPLA3 rs738409-G, TM6SF2 rs58542926-T, and MAU2 rs58489806-T). We screened first-order radiomic features in the full cohort and then focused the primary analysis on 77 treatment-naive patients whose tumor morphology had not been modified by therapy. Patients were stratified into at-risk (≥1 risk allele, n=52) and wild-type (no risk alleles, n=25) groups. Eighteen first-order radiomic features were screened using the Mann-Whitney U test and AUC analysis. The leading feature, kurtosis, was then subjected to univariate and multivariate analysis for clinical and imaging features to identify any confounding effect. In addition, a 10-fold cross-validated cutpoint stability, sensitivity analysis, and Cox/Kaplan-Meier survival analysis were also conducted. Results Among 18 features, kurtosis best distinguished at-risk from wild-type genotypes in treatment-naive patients (AUC = 0.67, p=0.014), with wild-type tumors showing more uniform, sharply peaked intensity patterns. Tumor volume correlated modestly with kurtosis (Spearman's ρ=0.45, p<0.0001), but volume alone did not discriminate genotype (Mann-Whitney U, p=0.3994). The genotype-kurtosis association remained significant after adjusting for volume and shape (ANCOVA, p=0.029) and strengthened after adjusting for nine clinical/demographic covariates (p=0.003), indicating kurtosis reflects biological information beyond tumor size. The empirical cutpoint was stable across 10-fold cross-validation (mean=3.35, SD = 0.05), and results were unchanged in sensitivity analysis. Kurtosis was not associated with overall survival (Cox HR = 1.19, p=0.13). No genotype-related discrimination was observed in the pooled full cohort, consistent with treatment-related alteration of tumor texture. Conclusions In a cohort of 210 genetically profiled patients with HCC, genotype-related radiomic features were not apparent when treated and untreated tumors were analyzed together. However, restricting the analysis to the treatment-naive subgroup (n=77) revealed tumor kurtosis as a reproducible, biologically plausible first-order imaging correlate of established HCC genetic risk status.

title: The clinical value of ultrasound radiomics combined with clinical data nomogram in predicting cervical lymph node metastasis of papillary thyroid carcinoma.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the predictive value of a nomogram incorporating ultrasound and clinical features for cervical lymph node metastasis (CLNM) in patients with thyroid cancer. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on patients pathologically diagnosed with papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) between April 2024 and January 2025. Radiomics features were extracted from two-dimensional thyroid ultrasound images, and feature selection was performed using the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO). Five classifiers were compared, and logistic regression was selected to construct the radiomics model. A clinical-radiomics model integrating the radiomics score and clinical predictors, together with a standalone clinical model, was developed using multivariable logistic regression. Model discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility were evaluated in a held-out internal validation set. Results Sex, Radscore, age, and thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) levels were identified as independent predictors of CLNM in patients with PTC. Based on these variables, radiomics, clinical, and clinical radiomics models were constructed; the models achieved area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.735, 0.792, and 0.867, respectively, in the validation set. DeLong's test and decision curve analysis (DCA) demonstrated that the clinical radiomics model outperformed the radiomics model in the validation set, offering a higher net clinical benefit. Conclusion A nomogram integrating ultrasound imaging and clinical data effectively predicts the risk of CLNM in patients with PTC and may assist clinicians in developing individualized treatment strategies.

title: Deep learning with interactive segmentation for risk stratification of cystic renal lesions on tri-phase CT: a multicenter study.
abstract: Background Accurate preoperative risk stratification of cystic renal lesions (CRLs) remains a clinical challenge, primarily due to morphological overlap which often leads to the overtreatment of indolent cysts. To address this, we developed and validated an integrated deep learning framework that combines interactive segmentation with tri-phase CT feature integration to refine malignancy prediction. Methods This retrospective multicenter study enrolled 434 patients with CRLs from four institutions, partitioned into training (n=195), validation (n=100), and external test (n=139) cohorts. The reference standard was histopathological diagnosis or ≥4 years of radiological stability. For volumetric segmentation, we implemented an interactive 'human-in-the-loop' Swin UNETR model. To integrate complementary information across the three CT phases, we then deployed a Tri-Phase-Channel (TPC) Perceiver architecture to integrate features extracted by parallel SEResNet50 backbones from unenhanced, corticomedullary, and nephrographic CT phases. Diagnostic performance was evaluated against the single-phase SEResNet50 models and the Bosniak classification version 2019 using the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC) and Decision Curve Analysis (DCA). Results In the external test cohort, the interactive segmentation model yielded a Dice score of 0.890. For malignancy prediction, the TPC-Perceiver attained an AUC of 0.969 (95% CI: 0.911-1.000), significantly outperforming the Bosniak classification version 2019 (AUC 0.884; p =0.016 ). At the fixed probability threshold of 0.5, the model achieved a sensitivity of 94.4% and a specificity of 96.7%, compared with 100.0% and 76.9%, respectively, for the clinical standard. Furthermore, decision curve analysis indicated that the deep learning framework conferred greater net benefit across a broad range of threshold probabilities. Conclusion The integrated framework showed favorable performance for cystic renal lesion risk stratification. Exploratory pairwise AUC comparisons favored the TPC Perceiver over the single-phase models and the clinical Bosniak v2019 assessment, while its AUC was comparable to that of the previous SETD model. The sensitivity-specificity profile observed at the fixed threshold suggests potential value in reducing false-positive risk stratification. Larger prospective multicenter studies are required before clinical implementation.

title: A multimodal deep learning radiomics nomogram integrating clinicopathological features for predicting pathological complete response after neoadjuvant therapy in triple-negative breast cancer: a multicenter retrospective study.
abstract: Background Accurate noninvasive estimation of pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant therapy (NAT) in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) may support multidisciplinary discussions, but multimodal MRI-ultrasound evidence remains limited. We developed and externally validated a clinicopathological deep learning radiomics nomogram and explored its potential auxiliary value in a strictly hypothetical post-hoc surgical-planning scenario. Methods With institutional review-board approval and waived consent, this retrospective multicenter diagnostic accuracy study included 436 biopsy-proven TNBC patients who underwent NAT and surgery: Center 1 training cohort (n = 268) and internal validation cohort (n = 86), plus historical cases from cooperating Centers 2-3 for external validation (n = 82). pCR was defined as ypT0/is ypN0. Pretreatment dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI), diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI)/apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps, T2-weighted imaging (T2WI), and B-mode ultrasound were analyzed. Intratumoral and 5-mm peritumoral ring radiomics features were extracted and selected by LASSO. DenseNet-121 extracted modality-specific deep features, fused using multi-head self-attention. Age, tumor size, Ki-67, tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs), cT/N stage, and histological grade were integrated with imaging scores in a logistic-regression nomogram. Parameters and thresholds were locked after Center 1 development and applied once to external data. No model output was used clinically. Feature standardization and ComBat harmonization parameters were strictly locked to the training cohort before application to validation data. Results pCR occurred in 182/436 patients (41.7%). The nomogram achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) of 0.917 (95% CI, 0.881-0.947) in training, 0.883 (0.814-0.937) in internal validation, and 0.856 (0.773-0.921) in external validation, exceeding clinical (external AUC, 0.721), radiomics (0.786), and deep learning (0.819) models. External sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy at the locked threshold were 0.765, 0.813, and 0.793, respectively. Calibration was acceptable (slope, 0.93; intercept, -0.06; Brier score, 0.16). Decision curve analysis showed net benefit for thresholds of 0.20-0.70. Multi-threshold analysis revealed that a high-specificity threshold (0.65) yielded a positive predictive value of 0.85, potentially identifying a subset of patients with very high confidence of achieving pCR. Compared with the clinical model, external reclassification improved (continuous net reclassification improvement [NRI], 0.34; integrated discrimination improvement [IDI], 0.11; P = 0.003 and P = 0.008, respectively). Conclusion Among the few multicenter TNBC studies combining MRI, ultrasound, intratumoral/peritumoral radiomics, and attention-based deep learning, this nomogram showed good retrospective accuracy for pCR prediction after NAT. The model is presented as an aid for pCR prediction and preoperative stratification rather than as direct support for surgical decision-making. Prospective validation and clinical-impact studies are required before implementation.

title: Vascular habitat analysis using dynamic susceptibility contrast-enhanced perfusion MRI for differentiating glioblastoma from solitary brain metastases.
abstract: Objective To investigate tumor vascular habitat parameters based on dynamic susceptibility contrast-enhanced perfusion-weighted imaging (DSC-PWI) for differentiating glioblastoma (GBM) from solitary brain metastasis (SBM). Methods In this single-center retrospective study, imaging data from 141 patients with pathologically or clinically confirmed malignant brain tumors (74 GBM, 67 SBM) were analyzed. The hemodynamic tissue signature (HTS) method was used to segment the lesions and construct four tumor vascular habitats: high angiogenic tumor (HAT), low angiogenic tumor (LAT), potentially infiltrated peripheral edema (IPE), and vasogenic peripheral edema (VPE). Pearson correlation analysis was used to quantify the correlations among habitat hemodynamic parameters. title: Mixed epithelial and stromal tumor of the kidney with prominent peritumoral adipose tissue: a case report radiologically mimicking angiomyolipoma with epithelial cysts.
abstract: Mixed epithelial and stromal tumor of the kidney (MEST) is a rare renal neoplasm with biphasic differentiation comprising epithelial and stromal components. It typically appears as a mixed cystic-solid mass on imaging, and the prognosis is favorable in the vast majority of cases. We report a case of MEST with a prominent fat component on imaging: a 54-year-old woman was admitted with a 1-month history of left flank distension and pain. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) showed a mixed cystic-solid mass at the lower pole of the left kidney, with a prominent low-attenuation fat-density area surrounding the mass. Preoperatively, the lesion was considered an unusual angiomyolipoma with epithelial cysts (AMLEC). Because the lesion was small, located at the lower pole, and relatively well circumscribed, the patient underwent laparoscopic left partial nephrectomy. Postoperative histopathologic examination confirmed that the left renal mass was benign; however, immunohistochemistry (IHC) demonstrated positivity for EMA and PCK in the epithelial component and for PR and ER in the stromal component, supporting a diagnosis of MEST. The adipose tissue submitted separately with the tumor was located around the tumor and could not be definitively confirmed as an intratumoral component. This case demonstrates that MEST may also exhibit prominent adipose tissue on imaging and illustrates the diagnostic pitfall in which fat-related imaging findings cause MEST to mimic AMLEC, making the early distinction between MEST and cystic change in fat-containing renal tumors challenging.

title: Retroauricular approach for carotid body tumor resection: a case report.
abstract: Introduction Carotid body tumors (CBTs) are rare and highly vascular paragangliomas arising at the carotid bifurcation. Surgical resection remains the standard treatment for CBTs. However, the conventional transcervical approach inevitably leaves a visible cervical scar, which may negatively affect quality of life in patients with cosmetic concerns. Case presentation A 27-year-old woman presented with a progressively enlarging right neck mass over a 6-month period. Ultrasonography demonstrated a hypervascular lesion surrounding the carotid arteries, and fine-needle aspiration was avoided because of the vascular nature of the tumor. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed a 4-cm enhancing mass at the carotid bifurcation, highly suggestive of a CBT. Because the patient expressed concern regarding a visible cervical scar, a retroauricular approach was selected after thorough discussion of its potential risks and benefits. The operation was performed by a head and neck surgeon with intraoperative assistance from a vascular surgeon. Complete tumor resection was successfully achieved despite the need for repair of two small arterial defects encountered during tumor mobilization. The operative time was 300 minutes, and the estimated blood loss was 900 mL. The postoperative course was uneventful, and no major complications or tumor recurrence were observed during 12 months of follow-up. The patient reported satisfaction with the cosmetic outcome, although no objective cosmetic assessment was performed. Conclusion In carefully selected patients with Shamblin type I or II CBT, the retroauricular approach may represent a feasible hidden-scar alternative to the conventional transcervical approach.

title: Ultrasonic manifestations of diffuse pericardial mesothelioma masquerading as pericardial effusion: a case report.
abstract: Background Primary pericardial mesothelioma (PPM) is an exceedingly rare, highly invasive cardiac neoplasm with insidious onset and non-specific clinical symptoms. Due to the lack of typical early manifestations and effective routine diagnostic methods, PPM is often misdiagnosed and missed, resulting in delayed treatment and poor prognosis. Case presentation A 42-year-old male presented with 6 months of recurrent chest tightness and pain, worsening over 2 months, and two prior admissions for unexplained pericardial effusion. On admission, he had tachycardia, distant heart sounds, bilateral lower extremity edema, and a 3×2 cm hard, fixed left supraclavicular lymph node. Imaging confirmed pericardial effusion with abnormal pericardial lesions. Ultrasound-guided pericardiocentesis yielded only a small amount of red jelly-like material, with cytology suggesting epithelioid neoplastic cells. Supraclavicular lymph node biopsy confirmed metastatic malignant mesothelioma. Nivolumab immunotherapy showed no improvement. Pericardial tumor resection revealed diffuse, fish-flesh-like tumor invading the myocardium and great vessels. Final pathology confirmed epithelioid-type PPM. Conclusion Patients with recurrent unexplained pericardial effusion and atypical sonographic features, such as flocculent echoes and irregular pericardial thickening, should raise suspicion for PPM. Early recognition of these signs and timely pathological confirmation are critical to avoid diagnostic delays and may improve outcomes.
