title: Non-invasive preoperative MRI-based deep transfer learning radiomics model for predicting meningioma brain invasion.
abstract: Background Current preoperative assessment of meningioma brain invasion (BI) demands imaging analytical frameworks that optimize computational efficiency while capturing multidimensional tumor-pathology correlations. Building upon the inherent advantages of 2.5D MRI in synthesizing multiplanar biological data with manageable processing loads, this study innovatively integrates deep transfer learning (DTL), a technique bridging pretrained network knowledge with target domain adaptation, to systematically identify tumor-invasive biological signatures and develop an optimized predictive system using preoperative contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging (CE-T1WI). Methods This retrospective study enrolled 674 patients with pathologically confirmed meningiomas, including 53 with BI and 621 without BI. The cohort was stratified into a training set and an independent test set. Tumor regions of interest (ROIs) were delineated on CE-T1WI, and radiomics and DTL features were extracted. Radiomics and DTL features were fused via early fusion, followed by feature selection. Within the training cohort, five-fold cross-validation was performed, with SMOTE applied exclusively to the training portion of each fold; validation folds and the independent test set retained their original class distributions. Results The effectiveness of the models was compared using the area under the ROC curve (AUC). In the training set, ComM achieved an AUC of 0.977, while in the test set, its AUC reached 0.935. ComM demonstrated the best performance (training set: AUCComM > AUCDTLRM > AUCRadM > AUCClinM > AUCDTLM; test set: AUCComM > AUCDTLRM > AUCRadM > AUCDTLM > AUCClinM), showing excellent preoperative predictive capability for meningioma BI. The Hosmer-Lemeshow test indicated good model fit, and the calibration curve revealed that ComM was closest to the ideal curve. Conclusion ClinM, RadM, DTLM, DTLRM, and ComM based on 2.5D CE-T1WI all exhibited good performance in predicting meningioma BI. The clinical-radiomics-DTL fusion model (ComM) demonstrated the highest efficacy, suggesting that DTL provides additional features correlated with meningioma BI that differ from radiomics features. This model shows potential clinical utility for preoperative prediction; however, further external validation in larger multicenter cohorts is required before clinical implementation.

title: Multiparametric MRI-based habitat and peritumoral radiomics integrating semi-automated segmentation for preoperative prediction of high-grade prostate cancer: a dual-center study.
abstract: Background This study aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine learning framework that combines semi-automated segmentation, intratumoral habitats derived from multiparametric MRI (mpMRI), and multiscale peritumoral radiomics to predict high-grade prostate cancer (HGPCa) before surgery. Methods This retrospective dual-center study involved 274 patients, comprising 208 from Center 1 for development and 66 from Center 2 for external test. The clinical and imaging variables included patient age, serum PSA, fPSA, PSAD, maximum tumor diameter, PI-RADS scores, and anatomical zone distribution (PZ vs. TZ). The development cohort was randomly divided into a training cohort (n = 145) and an internal validation cohort (n = 63). Intratumoral habitats were delineated using semi-automated segmentation and unsupervised K-means clustering, while peritumoral radiomic features were extracted from concentric 1-, 3-, and 5-mm shells. Predictive classifiers were optimized through machine learning algorithms, particularly a multilayer perceptron (MLP) for the habitat signature. A combined clinical-radiomics nomogram was constructed, with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) employed to enhance model interpretability. Subgroup analyses were performed to assess the discriminative performance of the combined nomogram across the peripheral zone (PZ) and transition zone (TZ). Results The combined nomogram exhibited superior diagnostic performance, achieving AUCs of 0.914, 0.903, and 0.797 in the training cohort, internal validation cohort, and external test cohort, respectively. The MLP-based habitat model showed good discriminative performance, with AUCs of 0.896, 0.897, and 0.782 across the training cohort, internal validation cohort, and external test cohort, respectively. Among the peritumoral regions, the 5-mm shell demonstrated the best discriminative performance. SHAP analysis identified Habitat 1 Shape Sphericity as the most influential feature. Subgroup analysis demonstrated the discriminatory ability of the combined nomogram in both the PZ (AUC: 0.796) and TZ (AUC: 0.753) subgroups. Conclusion The integration of semi-automated segmentation-based habitat analysis and peritumoral radiomics provides a promising approach for preoperative risk stratification of prostate cancer.

title: Liquid biopsy using circulating miRNAs for the identification of recurrence-associated biomarkers in glioblastoma CNS WHO grade 4.
abstract: Introduction Glioblastoma CNS WHO Grade 4 (GBM) is associated with poor prognosis and high recurrence rates despite the current therapeutic approaches. Conventional imaging, in particular Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), is primarily used during follow-up to detect tumor recurrence but has limited ability to distinguish recurrence from therapy-related changes, such as tissue necrosis and postoperative scar tissue. Liquid biopsy using circulating tumor-specific serological biomarkers, such as miRNAs, provides a gene expression signature for early identification of GBM recurrence. This pilot "proof-of-concept" study investigated the potential of circulating tumor-derived miRNA in whole blood samples for early detection of tumor recurrence. Methods In a previous whole-transcriptome screening (NGS) study, whole-blood samples (n = 33) from seven patients and tumor biopsies (n = 4) were used to identify biomarkers. Corresponding to tumor surgery and recurrence, miRNA expression was examined in pre-surgical blood samples and tumor tissues. In whole blood, we investigated whether a pattern could be identified indicating post-surgery downregulation, consistent with reduced tumor burden, followed by a return to pre-surgery levels at recurrence. We identified 1-19 miRNA species per patient (a total of 72 miRNAs) showing this pattern. In this manuscript, we present the qRT-PCR validation results. The 45 most promising miRNAs identified by NGS study were selected and quantified using qRT-PCR. In addition, miR-21 was included as a promising candidate reported in the literature. To address challenges in miRNA normalization, five normalization strategies and unnormalized raw Ct values were compared. Results Two normalization approaches (median DCt normalization and unnormalized raw Ct values) showed no systematic bias. Depending on the normalization method, the agreement between NGS and qRT-PCR ranged from 23.6 to 27.9%. Although the concordance between NGS and qRT-PCR was low at the individual-patient level, qRT-PCR identified a common set of 24 miRNAs differentially regulated across patients. Notably, miR-424-3p and miR-362-5p were shared by five of seven patients, followed by miR-1307-3p and miR-22-5p , each shared by four patients. Interestingly, miR-21 did not show the predefined recurrence-associated pattern in any patient. Discussion Blood-based miRNA profiling may complement imaging in longitudinal monitoring of GBM patients, although clinical benefits have not been confirmed, and validation in a larger independent cohort is required.

Introduction

Glioblastoma CNS WHO Grade 4 (GBM) is associated with poor prognosis and high recurrence rates despite the current therapeutic approaches. Conventional imaging, in particular Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), is primarily used during follow-up to detect tumor recurrence but has limited ability to distinguish recurrence from therapy-related changes, such as tissue necrosis and postoperative scar tissue. Liquid biopsy using circulating tumor-specific serological biomarkers, such as miRNAs, provides a gene expression signature for early identification of GBM recurrence. This pilot "proof-of-concept" study investigated the potential of circulating tumor-derived miRNA in whole blood samples for early detection of tumor recurrence.

Methods

In a previous whole-transcriptome screening (NGS) study, whole-blood samples (n = 33) from seven patients and tumor biopsies (n = 4) were used to identify biomarkers. Corresponding to tumor surgery and recurrence, miRNA expression was examined in pre-surgical blood samples and tumor tissues. In whole blood, we investigated whether a pattern could be identified indicating post-surgery downregulation, consistent with reduced tumor burden, followed by a return to pre-surgery levels at recurrence. We identified 1-19 miRNA species per patient (a total of 72 miRNAs) showing this pattern. In this manuscript, we present the qRT-PCR validation results. The 45 most promising miRNAs identified by NGS study were selected and quantified using qRT-PCR. In addition, miR-21 was included as a promising candidate reported in the literature. To address challenges in miRNA normalization, five normalization strategies and unnormalized raw Ct values were compared.

Results

Two normalization approaches (median DCt normalization and unnormalized raw Ct values) showed no systematic bias. Depending on the normalization method, the agreement between NGS and qRT-PCR ranged from 23.6 to 27.9%. Although the concordance between NGS and qRT-PCR was low at the individual-patient level, qRT-PCR identified a common set of 24 miRNAs differentially regulated across patients. Notably, miR-424-3p and miR-362-5p were shared by five of seven patients, followed by miR-1307-3p and miR-22-5p, each shared by four patients. Interestingly, miR-21 did not show the predefined recurrence-associated pattern in any patient.

Discussion

Blood-based miRNA profiling may complement imaging in longitudinal monitoring of GBM patients, although clinical benefits have not been confirmed, and validation in a larger independent cohort is required.

title: A prospective pilot study of urine microRNA as a biomarker of urinary radiation toxicity following MRI-guided prostate stereotactic body radiotherapy.
abstract: Introduction Urinary toxicities are common following prostate radiotherapy and can impair quality of life. New biomarkers are needed that can predict the risk of urinary toxicity following MRI guided stereotactic body radiotherapy (MR-SBRT) to assist with selection of the most appropriate radiotherapy treatment approach. We aimed to identify urine miRNA biomarkers of radiation-induced urinary toxicities. Methods Ten patients undergoing MR-SBRT were enrolled on a prospective biorepository protocol and urine specimens were collected before, at the final fraction and 2-4 months following radiotherapy. RNA was isolated and microRNA sequencing was performed followed by qPCR for confirmation of microRNA expression changes. Differences in microRNA expression were assessed with regard to timepoint, cancer risk category and urinary toxicity. Results Both sequencing and qPCR showed that expressions of miR-26a-5p and miR-95-3p decrease during MR-SBRT and increase during early follow up. miR-204-3p and miR-192-5p changed differently in patients with and without urinary radiation toxicity. Expression of miR-375-3p was lower in patients with higher risk category (NCCN unfavorable intermediate to high risk or recurrent/metastatic) at all timepoints and decreased during and after MR-SBRT, especially in patients with a lower risk category (NCCN low to favorable intermediate risk) of prostate cancer. Discussion Urine microRNA analysis is feasible and may identify biomarkers linked to radiation-induced urinary toxicity and prostate cancer severity. The findings of this pilot study are limited by the sample size and should be prospectively validated.

title: Relevance between patients' clinical factors and 4D-CT lung ventilation heterogeneity for evaluating the adoption of functional avoidance thoracic radiotherapy with a large patient database.
abstract: Objective Four-dimensional computed tomography (4D-CT)-guided functional-avoidance radiotherapy reduces radiation pneumonitis, but the lack of patient selection criteria limits its adoption. This study aimed to identify clinical predictors of lung ventilation heterogeneity and determine which patients derive the greatest dosimetric benefit from functional-avoidance planning. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 274 lung cancer patients. 4D-CT ventilation imaging was generated via deformable registration and a density-change algorithm, and the coefficient of variation (CoV) across six lung zones quantified heterogeneity. Clinical factors were assessed using Mann-Whitney U, Spearman, and multivariable logistic regression for three ventilation outcomes. Thirty-two patients were selected from CoV quartiles and re-planned with functional-avoidance plans; dosimetric parameters were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction applied to address multiple comparisons. Results Univariate analysis showed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and airway obstruction reduced bilateral mean ventilation, while central tumors impaired ipsilateral ventilation. Higher CoV was observed in stage III-IV versus I-II, central versus peripheral tumors, and patients with airway obstruction. Multivariable analysis identified airway obstruction as an independent predictor of elevated CoV (adjusted OR = 2.914, 95% CI: 1.315-6.454, P<0.05). Central location and advanced stage showed borderline significance, while COPD trended toward lower CoV. Dosimetrically, functional-avoidance plans reduced functional lung metrics in a heterogeneity-dependent manner. After FDR correction, key metrics (fMLD, fV10, fV20, fV30) remained significant in Group 1 (highest CoV; Q = 0.040-0.049), while significance diminished in lower CoV groups. Leave-one-out (LOO) sensitivity analysis confirmed fMLD and fV20 as robust endpoints. Furthermore, beam arrangement modifications were most frequent in Group 1 (5/8 patients) and absent in Group 4 (0/8), reflecting clinical optimization needs rather than confounding. Conclusions Ventilation heterogeneity is driven by tumor burden and airway patency. Patients with advanced stage, central tumors, or airway obstruction exhibit the strongest heterogeneity and may represent appropriate candidates for functional-avoidance radiotherapy in future prospective trials. However, as this replanning study lacked clinical follow-up for radiation pneumonitis, these findings reflect dosimetric rather than confirmed clinical patient-level benefit. Notably, CoV quartiles were derived from internal median splits within this cohort and require external validation. This study provides a dosimetric basis for hypothesis-generating patient selection.

title: CBCT-based adaptive radiotherapy and automated radiotherapy decision-making systems: development and current status.
abstract: Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)-based adaptive radiotherapy (ART) has emerged as a promising strategy for addressing inter-fractional anatomical and physiological changes during treatment. By incorporating on-treatment imaging, ART enables treatment plans to be adapted to the anatomy of the day, with the potential to improve target coverage and reduce dose exposure to organs at risk (OARs). However, routine implementation remains constrained by the limited image quality of CBCT, uncertainties in dose calculation, labour-intensive workflows and the lack of reliable criteria for determining when adaptation is clinically necessary. This review summarises the development, current status and future prospects of CBCT-based ART, with particular emphasis on artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted automated delineation and automated radiotherapy decision-making systems. CBCT is widely available on modern linear accelerators and remains the most practical imaging basis for ART in many centres. Nevertheless, poor soft-tissue contrast, noise, artefacts, field-of-view truncation and unstable Hounsfield unit values limit its performance in target delineation and dose reconstruction. Recent advances in image-quality enhancement, deformable image registration and synthetic CT generation have partially addressed these limitations. AI-based auto-segmentation models, including convolutional neural networks, Transformers, generative adversarial networks and diffusion models, have demonstrated increasingly favourable geometric accuracy and workflow efficiency. Automated decision-making systems can advise clinicians whether treatment-plan adaptation is required and how it should be implemented according to each patient's circumstances, representing a prerequisite for more efficient ART. Current research has mainly focused on two approaches: adaptation triggered by predefined dosimetric thresholds, and artificial-intelligence-based models that learn from prior knowledge and predict potential dosimetric changes for the current patient based on previous experience. Both approaches have their respective strengths and limitations, but require further refinement, including the systematic exploration of decision thresholds. Moreover, the realisation of fully automated adaptive radiotherapy will require the integration of additional systems, including automated treatment planning and automated QA. Overall, CBCT-based ART assisted by AI is technically feasible and may improve dosimetric quality and treatment efficiency. Future progress requires improved CBCT-specific algorithms, integrated automated planning and QA, multicentre validation, standardised safety frameworks and stronger evidence of clinical benefit.

title: Multiple sclerosis relapse following gamma knife radiosurgery for meningioma in a patient treated with natalizumab: case report.
abstract: Objectives We describe a case of a patient with multiple sclerosis (MS) stable on natalizumab who developed widespread gadolinium-enhancing lesions and clinical relapse seven and eight months after gamma knife radiosurgery (GKRS) for left cerebellar convexity meningioma. We explore how increased blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability post-GKRS could potentially interfere with the lymphocyte anti-trafficking effect of natalizumab and result in new central nervous system (CNS) inflammation distant from the radiation site. Methods Comprehensive analysis of the patient's chart, brain and spine imaging, serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) profiles was conducted. We compiled a graphical representation of treatment changes, radiologic findings, and GKRS initiation within one timeframe. We conducted a structured literature review to support the discussion of this case and hypothesize possible pathophysiological mechanisms contributing to clinical and radiological findings. Results Seven months after GKRS, follow-up brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated multiple gadolinium-enhancing lesions in both cerebral hemispheres, and repeat imaging one month later revealed new gadolinium-enhancing lesions, correlating with the patient's clinical relapse. Alternative causes of disease progression, including radiation-induced demyelination, radionecrosis, opportunistic infections, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), and development of anti-natalizumab antibodies, were explored and considered less likely. The patient was switched to ofatumumab with subsequent clinical and radiological stability. Discussion Given extensive new inflammatory lesions far from the GKRS site, it seems unlikely that the sole mechanism was radiation-induced neurotoxicity. We hypothesize that late delayed radiation side effects caused by GKRS may have enabled peripheral lymphocytes to enter the CNS, counteracting the effects of natalizumab on blocking lymphocyte trafficking through the BBB and possibly contributing to MS relapse.

title: HSV-Net: hybrid state-space and self-supervised vision fusion with progressive contour learning for CT pulmonary nodule segmentation.
abstract: Accurate voxel-level segmentation of pulmonary nodules on chest CT is needed for diameter and volume measurement, growth tracking, and quantitative assessment in lung cancer screening. The task remains difficult: nodules vary in attenuation, size, and contact with vessels or pleura, and clinically relevant morphology often lies in a thin, ambiguous margin. Existing systems commonly trade contour fidelity for speed-large prompt-driven foundation models can be accurate but slow, whereas compact CNN or SSM decoders are efficient yet tend to smooth spiculated and ground-glass borders. We propose HSV-Net (Hybrid State-space-Vision Network), a dual-stream 3D network that is prompt-free after nodule localization: an SSM3D stream provides whole-patch context with linear-complexity state-space blocks, and an OrthoLoRA stream adapts frozen DINOv2 features on axial, coronal, and sagittal slices. A Hybrid Gated Mixer (HGM) fuses the two streams before FPN decoding, and Progressive Contour Learning (PCL) supervises overlap, signed-distance-field geometry, and uncertainty-weighted contour refinement. On a 10-patient QIN Lung CT/QIN-LungCT-Seg development subset ( n = 12 tumors; nested patient-level 5-fold CV), HSV-Net obtained the highest mean Dice (90.1% ± 1.0%; 95% CI [88.9, 91.3]) and Boundary F1 (86.3% ± 1.3%) among the compared methods on 128 × 128 × 64 patches, with a latency of 58 ms. A standard full-volume nnU-Net v2 baseline reached 88.6% ± 1.0% Dice on the same QIN folds, still below HSV-Net. On an independent LIDC-IDRI benchmark with expert volumetric consensus masks (186 patients/294 nodules; patient-level 5-fold CV within LIDC, not QIN→LIDC transfer), HSV-Net achieved 87.8% ± 1.1% Dice and 83.6% ± 1.3% Boundary F1, outperforming full-volume nnU-Net (87.1% ± 1.0% Dice). LUNA16 was retained only as a proxy size/localization check with diameter-matched spherical references, not as contour external validation.

title: Low CT-derived vertebral attenuation as a prognostic factor in hepatocellular carcinoma patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors.
abstract: Background Computed tomography (CT)-derived vertebral attenuation has been recognized as an indicator of prognosis for patients undergoing tumor removal, liver transplant, or transcatheter arterial chemoembolization (TACE) therapy, but similar research has not been reported in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). This study aims to explore the prognostic value of CT-derived vertebral attenuation in HCC patients treated with ICIs. Methods This retrospective study included HCC patients who received ICI treatment at Wuhan Union Hospital between July 2020 and March 2024. CT-derived vertebral attenuation was assessed by measuring mean Hounsfield unit (HU) values in the center of the first lumbar vertebra (L1) on non-contrast CT scans. Based on the optimal cutoff value derived from X-tile software, patients were classified into the CT-derived L1 attenuation-low group (≤100 HU) and the CT-derived L1 attenuation-high group (>100 HU). A comparison of the baseline characteristics of the two groups was made, followed by a propensity score matching (PSM) analysis to balance the variables. The objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR) were calculated for both groups, and Kaplan-Meier survival curves and Cox regression models were used to analyze overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS). Results The cohort consisted of 357 patients, divided into the L1 attenuation-low group (n = 112) and the L1 attenuation-high group (n = 245). Among all patients, 30.0% (107/357) achieved complete or partial response. After PSM analysis, both groups contained 91 patients. The L1 attenuation-low group had shorter OS (hazard ratio [HR], 1.73; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.15-2.60; P = 0.008) and PFS (HR, 1.47; 95% CI, 1.04-2.08; P = 0.030) than the L1 attenuation-high group. Conclusion CT-derived L1 attenuation can stratify survival risk for HCC patients undergoing ICI treatment.

title: Boundary-aware geometric Mamba network for breast tumor segmentation in 3D MRI.
abstract: Introduction Accurate breast tumor segmentation in Dynamic Contrast-Enhanced Magnetic Resonance Imaging (DCE-MRI) is important for reliable diagnosis and treatment planning. However, complex tumor morphology, diverse spatial structures, and indistinct boundaries remain challenging for existing segmentation methods. Convolutional neural network-based methods have limited ability to model long-range dependencies, while Transformer-based methods often introduce substantial computational overhead. Although Mamba-based approaches provide an efficient alternative, conventional scanning strategies may suffer from directional bias and insufficiently capture three-dimensional structural variations. Methods We propose a Boundary-Aware Geometric Mamba Network (BAGMNet) for three-dimensional breast tumor segmentation. BAGMNet establishes a structural representation learning framework that combines geometric modeling, multi-directional state-space propagation, and boundary-aware feature refinement. The Geometric Mamba Encoder constructs complementary spatial representations through multiple geometric transformations, while the Multi-directional Selective State Space module enhances three-dimensional dependency modeling and alleviates the directional bias of conventional Mamba scanning. The Gated State-space Fusion and Adaptive Skip Recalibration modules further integrate local structural details with global contextual information and enhance boundary-related representations during feature propagation. Results Extensive experiments were conducted on the ISPY1 and Yunnan breast MRI datasets. BAGMNet achieved Dice scores of 70.34% and 79.14%, with average surface distances of 9.79 mm and 8.96 mm on the ISPY1 and Yunnan datasets, respectively. Compared with representative convolutional neural network-, Transformer-, and Mamba-based methods, BAGMNet achieved competitive performance in both regional segmentation accuracy and boundary localization.

title: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma manifesting as a solitary metastasis to the skeletal muscle of the scapular region accompanied by invasion of the adjacent bone while on PD-1 inhibitor maintenance therapy: a case report.
abstract: Cervical cancer is a common malignancy in women worldwide, with distant metastases frequently occurring in the lungs, liver, bones, and lymph nodes. However, this case report presents an extremely rare isolated metastasis to the left scapular region,specifically located between the supraspinatus and the trapezius muscles, in a patient with locally advanced cervical squamous cell carcinoma who developed this lesion during maintenance therapy with a programmed death receptor-1 (PD-1) inhibitor after completing concurrent chemoradiotherapy. The clinical presentation of this metastatic lesion was atypical and posed a significant diagnostic challenge; however, multimodal imaging (MRI, PET/CT) and histopathological examination ultimately confirmed the diagnosis of cervical cancer metastasis. This finding underscores the necessity of maintaining a high level of vigilance for metastases in atypical sites, even in the era of immunotherapy. To manage this rare presentation, a multidisciplinary team developed a comprehensive treatment strategy centered on surgical resection, followed by postoperative adjuvant radiotherapy administered concurrently with chemotherapy and anti-angiogenic therapy(Q3W) consisting of paclitaxel 135 mg/m², cisplatin 50 mg/m², and bevacizumab 10 mg/kg. The patient remained recurrence-free at 13 months, suggesting that a multimodal combined local and systemic strategy may be feasible for selected patients with solitary muscle metastasis. This case not only adds to the clinical understanding of rare metastases in cervical cancer but also demonstrates that tumors can still metastasize to atypical sites under immunotherapy. These findings highlight the need for vigilance regarding metastases at atypical sites during immunotherapy. Any underlying mechanism-including immune editing and clonal evolution-remains speculative in the absence of paired molecular data and requires further validation.

title: Clinical and radiological features of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome in children: a retrospective study.
abstract: Background Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is an uncommon but critical neurological emergency in children. Data on Chinese pediatric cohorts remain limited. Objective To analyze the clinical features, imaging findings, and treatment of PRES in children to improve early diagnosis and management. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 10 children diagnosed with PRES from March 2016 to January 2025. Results The patients included 7 males and 3 females, aged 3-13 years (mean 7.5 years). The main underlying diseases were acute lymphoblastic leukemia (3 cases) and nephrotic syndrome (3 cases). Eight children (80%) had hypertension, 6 (60%) had hypoalbuminemia, and 8 received glucocorticoids or immunosuppressants. The main symptoms were headache, seizures, impaired consciousness, and visual disturbances. Cranial MRI showed symmetrical long T1 and long T2 signals in bilateral posterior cerebral white matter. After comprehensive treatment including antihypertensive, anticonvulsant, and dehydration therapy, all symptoms resolved and lesions disappeared on follow-up imaging without sequelae. Conclusion Pediatric PRES is an acute reversible disorder associated with hypertension and immunosuppressive therapy. Early MRI diagnosis and prompt intervention can significantly improve prognosis.

title: CuFormer U-Net: a transformer-enhanced multi-task network for cucumber leaf disease detection and segmentation.
abstract: Cucumber foliar symptoms reduce functional leaf area and complicate greenhouse scouting. This study presents CuFormer U-Net, a Transformer-enhanced multi-task network for three-class image-level classification on the 3,754-image Kaggle benchmark (healthy, powdery mildew, and downy mildew) and binary visible-symptom segmentation on a separate 400-image greenhouse cohort (200 healthy and 200 affected leaves). The greenhouse annotations comprise 2,705 rectangles (1,741 color-abnormality and 964 tissue-damage instances); rectangle-seeded lesion masks were manually refined for the dense-prediction experiments. The reported fixed-split point estimates were 96.7% accuracy, 96.3% macro precision, 95.8% macro recall, and 96.0% macro F1 for classification, and 92.4% mean image-wise Dice, 83.1% macro IoU, 93.2% foreground precision, and 91.7% foreground recall for segmentation. The complete internal-validation ablation configuration reached 93.1% Dice and 87.3% IoU. The available experiment archive does not contain independent-seed reruns, per-image predictions for inferential testing, annotator-level masks, quantitative results for the separate 100-image greenhouse stress-test cohort, or reproducible hardware profiling. Accordingly, all between-model differences are interpreted descriptively, the external cohort is not presented as formal external validation, and robustness and deployment claims have been moderated. CuFormer U-Net provides a technically motivated basis for joint recognition and spatial characterization, but confirmatory multi-run and multi-site evaluation is required. boundary refinement, cucumber leaf disease, multi-task learning, plant disease, precision agriculture, semantic segmentation, vision transformer.

title: Q-rung orthopair fuzzy framework for multimodal MRI image fusion and U-Net-based segmentation for brain tumor detection.
abstract: Medical image analysis is a significant research domain in contemporary healthcare systems, which helps to accurately diagnose diseases and support clinical decision-making. This domain consists of important operations, including image enhancement, fusion, segmentation, morphological processing, and denoising, which assist in the effective understanding of complex biomedical information. Multimodal image fusion and segmentation are particularly important among these processes, as they enable the integration of complementary diagnostic information and the clear interpretation of clinically meaningful structures. However, medical images often consist of uncertainty, noise, and incomplete pixel information, creating major challenges for conventional analytical techniques. To address these challenges, the present study introduces a q-rung orthopair fuzzy set (qROFS)-based framework for multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) fusion, subsequently a U-Net-based segmentation architecture for brain tumor detection. To effectively handle uncertainty and preserve important image information, the fusion strategy is designed based on q-rung orthopair fuzzy Hamacher t-norm and t-conorm operators to integrate complementary information in four different MRI modalities, including T1, T1ce, T2, and Flair. The resultant fused images are subsequently processed through a U-Net architecture to obtain precise tumor segmentation. Experiments conducted on the BraTS 2020 benchmark dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Across the four MRI modalities (T1, T1ce, T2, and Flair), the proposed fusion framework attains the best quantitative performance when compared to state-of-the-art methods with an SSIM of 0.9271, an MSSIM of 0.9481, a PSNR of 24.7130 dB, a low AMBE of 6.6779, a Correlation coefficient of 0.9583, an MI of 1.4097, and a UQI of 0.9767. A comparative evaluation with existing fuzzy set-based fusion models further assures the effectiveness of the proposed qROFS-based framework for multimodal MRI image fusion. Furthermore, the U-Net-based segmentation model achieves excellent performance, with an accuracy of 98.96%, a precision of 98.95%, a sensitivity of 98.94%, and a specificity of 99.65%.

title: Temporal phase coverage and patient cohort size in deep learning-based cardiac cine computed tomography angiography segmentation.
abstract: Background Annotating all phases of cine computed tomography angiography (CTA) is burdensome. We evaluated how temporal phase coverage and patient cohort size affect deep learning-based cardiac segmentation. Methods Twelve 3D U-Net models were trained using a 110-patient single-phase CTA dataset or a 20-patient, 20-phase cine CTA dataset. Phase-coverage ablations used one, two, or 20 phases; patient-count ablations were performed within both datasets. One cine patient was used for validation and four independent patients were used for testing. Five cardiac structures were evaluated using Dice and the 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95). Phase-wise and patient-level Dice consistency and structure-specific volumetric variability within and between subjects were assessed. Results Full cine training produced higher overall Dice (0.89 vs. 0.87) and lower overall HD95 (4.87 vs. 9.78 mm) than the single-phase reference (both p < 0.05). Right ventricular (RV) Dice was higher (0.91 vs. 0.84) and HD95 was lower (5.16 vs. 22.75 mm; both p < 0.05). The two-phase model achieved an overall Dice of 0.88 and an overall HD95 of 7.85 mm; neither metric differed significantly from the single-phase reference. HD95 generally increased with smaller cohorts, and both metrics deteriorated markedly in the five-patient configurations. Full cine training showed flatter phase-wise Dice profiles and lower across-phase variability. Between-subject volume differences exceeded phase-related within-subject differences for all structures (all p < 0.05). Conclusion In this cross-cohort comparison, full cine training showed higher overall Dice, lower overall HD95, and greater phase-wise consistency than single-phase training. The evaluated two-phase configuration may inform annotation-efficient cine CTA dataset design, but broader validation is needed.

The two-phase model achieved an overall Dice of 0.88 and an overall HD95 of 7.85 mm; neither metric differed significantly from the single-phase reference. HD95 generally increased with smaller cohorts, and both metrics deteriorated markedly in the five-patient configurations. Full cine training showed flatter phase-wise Dice profiles and lower across-phase variability. Between-subject volume differences exceeded phase-related within-subject differences for all structures (all p < 0.05).

Conclusion

In this cross-cohort comparison, full cine training showed higher overall Dice, lower overall HD95, and greater phase-wise consistency than single-phase training. The evaluated two-phase configuration may inform annotation-efficient cine CTA dataset design, but broader validation is needed.

title: Automated Nuchal Translucency analysis for early prenatal risk stratification.
abstract: Nuchal Translucency (NT) is a measurement taken from ultrasound images described as the gathering of fluid behind the fetus's neck, during 11-13 weeks. Increased Nuchal Translucency can lead to high risk of chromosomal abnormalities like Down Syndrome. The existing AI model may struggle to detect the subtle difference due to low resolution fetal movement, which can lead to errors in measurements and diagnosis. In addition, traditional NT measurement methods rely heavily on manual caliper placement, making the process operator-dependent and reducing consistency and automation. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an Enhanced Multi-Scale Spatial Temporal Graph Attention Network (EMSSTGAN) to predict the risk of chromosomal abnormalities in NT. Initially, the input images of NT are pre-processed using feature refinement attention network (FRANet) for denoising and Multi-Scale Attention Retinex Network (MARN) for contrast enhancement. NT detection is then performed by localizing the nuchal translucency region using bounding box annotations, followed by U-Net-based segmentation for precise extraction of the NT area. The Active Contour Model (ACM) is subsequently applied to measure the NT thickness based on boundary geometry. The thickness when compared with threshold values is used to identify the risk of chromosomal abnormalities as low, medium and high. The proposed model achieves an accuracy of 98.15%, an error of 1.85%, and a FDR of 2.44%, respectively.

title: Beyond diagnostic accuracy: navigating the artificial intelligence data tsunami toward value-based implementation in gastroenterology.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy has evolved from its early application in simple edge detection to highly sophisticated technologies designed to improve detection of neoplastic and preneoplastic lesions and support clinical decision-making. However, this rapid technological evolution has generated a " data tsunami " or " datanami ": an overwhelming and continuously expanding volume of information that, frequently, exceeds the ability of clinicians and patients to process, interpret, and apply it effectively. Substantial investments in AI have been driven by expectations of improved efficiency and reduced healthcare costs. Nevertheless, the metrics used to justify the adoption of AI-assisted diagnostic and therapeutic strategies remain inadequately standardized, leaving the true cost-effectiveness of these technologies uncertain. Current AI research in gastroenterology has primarily focused on improving diagnostic performance rather than evaluating long-term clinical outcomes or economic value. To address this limitation, investigators employ stochastic microsimulation models, which simulate individual patient trajectories and enable more robust assessments of cost-effectiveness. As the field progresses from AI to extended intelligence and, ultimately, intelligent assistance, the role of humans becomes increasingly central. Rather than replacing clinical judgment, AI should augment human expertise, with healthcare professionals serving as the critical link between technological innovation and meaningful clinical benefit. This review examines whether AI applications in GI diseases can be implemented cost-effectively in routine clinical practice for diagnosis and treatment. It further explores the indispensable human dimension of AI adoption, emphasizing accountability, reliability, ethical oversight, and responsible implementation as essential safeguards for current and future clinical applications.

title: The "Sandwich" technique using a lateral locking plate and intramedullary reconstruction plate with bone cement for osteoporotic proximal humerus fractures: a case series.
abstract: Introduction Although lateral locking plate fixation is widely used for displaced proximal humerus fractures, fixation failure remains a major concern in elderly osteoporotic patients, particularly when medial column defects are present. Poor cancellous bone quality reduces screw purchase, while medial comminution and metaphyseal bone voids weaken the ability of the proximal humerus to resist varus and axial loading. Existing augmentation methods address only part of this problem. Fibular strut allografts can provide intramedullary and medial support but may be limited by graft availability, size matching, cost, and technical complexity, and they do not directly reinforce the screw-bone interface of all proximal screws. Cement augmentation can improve screw purchase, but cement alone does not create a defined intramedullary support structure or reconstruct medial column bone defects. Therefore, a composite fixation strategy is needed to simultaneously provide lateral fixation, intramedullary support, medial column stability, enhanced screw purchase, and bone defect reconstruction. To address this clinical gap, we developed the "Sandwich" technique, which combines a lateral locking plate, an intramedullary reconstruction plate, PMMA bone cement, and allogeneic cancellous bone graft to create a multidirectional support construct. Methods Five patients with osteoporotic proximal humerus fractures and medial column defects were treated using the "Sandwich" technique. This construct consisted of a lateral locking plate, an intramedullary reconstruction plate, PMMA bone cement, and allogeneic cancellous bone graft. The lateral locking plate provided lateral fixation, whereas the intramedullary reconstruction plate provided internal structural support. PMMA bone cement was placed between the two plates to reinforce screw purchase and construct stability, and allogeneic cancellous bone graft was used to fill the residual metaphyseal and medial column defects. Results The mean operative time was 123.0 ± 16.1 min, with an average blood loss of 206.0 ± 85.3 mL, hospital stay of 8.4 ± 1.1 days, and mean hospitalization cost of 56,258.4 ± 6,152.1 CNY. At 12 months postoperatively, all fractures achieved radiographic union without loss of reduction, screw penetration, or varus collapse. The mean CMS was 87.0 ± 6.0 and the mean Neer score was 86.0 ± 6.1. No cases of avascular necrosis or fixation failure were observed. Conclusion The "Sandwich" technique provides strong medial and intramedullary support, improves screw fixation, and enhances overall biomechanical stability in osteoporotic proximal humerus fractures. It achieved excellent healing and functional recovery with minimal complications, representing a promising surgical alternative to traditional fibular graft-assisted fixation.

title: Jejunal intussusception following distal gastrectomy with Billroth I anastomosis: a case report.
abstract: A 41-year-old male patient presented with acute persistent abdominal pain for 4 h and was admitted to our hospital in October 2023. The patient had a height of 178 cm and a weight of 55 kg, with a precisely calculated body mass index (BMI) of 17.4 kg/m² and a body surface area of 1.73 m². He was diagnosed with acute gastric perforation and underwent emergency distal gastrectomy combined with Billroth I gastroduodenal anastomosis and intraoperative jejunal feeding tube placement. On postoperative day (POD) 19, the patient developed aggravated abdominal distension and paroxysmal abdominal pain without fever, vomiting, or diarrhea. Laboratory tests showed slightly elevated inflammatory markers and normal serum lactate, while abdominal computed tomography (CT) revealed typical intestinal intussusception and partial intestinal obstruction. Emergency re-laparotomy confirmed antegrade jejunojejunal intussusception located approximately 20 cm distal to the Treitz ligament, with an intussusception length of approximately 40 cm. Manual reduction was successfully performed without intestinal resection or intraoperative complications. The patient achieved uneventful gastrointestinal function recovery and was discharged on POD 12 after reoperation. No recurrence of intussusception was observed during 6 months of outpatient follow-up. This study reports a rare case of late-onset antegrade jejunojejunal intussusception following Billroth I gastrectomy. Combined effects of low BMI-related loose mesentery, intra-abdominal postoperative adhesions, and indwelling jejunal feeding tube were identified as potential associative risk factors rather than definitive causal factors. We aim to summarize the clinical characteristics, diagnostic strategies, and standardized prevention and treatment protocols of this rare postoperative complication to supplement relevant clinical evidence.

title: When should a laparoscopic cholecystectomy be performed after ERCP for common bile duct stones combined with gallbladder stones? A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
abstract: Background Gallstones combined with common bile duct stones are a common disease in biliary surgery. At present, for gallbladder stones with common bile duct stones, the globally recognized standard treatment is a step-by-step treatment of "endoscopy combined with surgery". First, more urgent and potentially life-threatening bile duct stones are treated, and then gallbladder stones are treated. However, after the common bile duct stones are successfully removed by ERCP, how long should laparoscopic cholecystectomy be performed at intervals? There is a dispute between "early" (defined as within 72 h after ERCP) and "delayed" (defined as 72 h after ERCP). The conclusion is not yet uniform. Objective To systematically analyze the efficacy and safety of early LC and delayed LC in patients with gallstones and common bile duct stones after ERCP, to provide current high-level evidence-based medical evidence for clinical decision-making, to help clinicians optimize the diagnosis and treatment process, to reduce the occurrence of adverse complications caused by treatment. Method PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Scopus, and other databases were searched to collect randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing early LC and delayed LC after ERCP from inception to December 2025. Two reviewers independently screened literature, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias of included studies using the Cochrane ROB evaluation tool. The RevMan 5.4 software was used to analyze the outcomes of each group. Unlike previous meta-analyses, this study only included randomized controlled trials and incorporated the latest ones. Moreover, the quality of each outcome indicator was evaluated using the GRADE method. Result This meta-analysis included 7 randomized controlled trials involving 593 patients (296 in the early LC group and 297 in the delayed LC group). Compared with the delayed LC group, the early LC group was associated with a significantly lower rate of conversion to open surgery ( RR = 0.35, 95 % CI : 0.17-0.68, P = 0.002), shorter operation time ( MD = -14.37 min, 95 % CI : -28.22 to -0.51, P = 0.04), shorter postoperative hospital stay ( MD = -0.81 days, 95 % CI : -1.20 to -0.42, P < 0.0001), and lower incidence of incision infection (RR = 0.21, 95 % CI : 0.07-0.61, P = 0.004). No significant difference was observed between the two groups in the incidence of bile leakage ( RD = -0.04, 95 % CI : -0.12-0.04, P = 0.30). Conclusion In conclusion, the available RCT evidence suggests that early LC following successful ERCP may provide clinical advantages over delayed LC, including lower conversion and infection rates and shorter operative and postoperative hospital stay. However, because of outcome-level heterogeneity, the limited number of included trials, and few bile-leakage events, these findings should be interpreted with caution and further verified in larger well-designed RCTs. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261395564, PROSPERO CRD420261395564.

title: Free flap selection strategies and advances in facial soft tissue defect reconstruction.
abstract: Reconstruction of facial soft tissue defects remains a demanding task in plastic, reconstructive, and head and neck surgery because the face combines aesthetic units with essential functions such as oral competence, speech, swallowing, breathing, eyelid protection, and facial expression. The severity, depth, and composition of the defect are the primary determinants of flap selection, especially when defects extend beyond skin and subcutaneous tissue to expose the oral cavity, pharynx, nasal cavity, skull base, or critical structures. This narrative review summarizes evidence and technical progress regarding free flap selection for facial soft tissue reconstruction. Literature was identified through PubMed, Web of Science, and Google Scholar using combinations of the terms "facial soft tissue defect," "free flap," "perforator flap," and "virtual surgical planning." Priority was given to systematic reviews, meta-analyses, clinical series, and studies published between 2019 and 2026, while classic microsurgical reports were retained when foundational. Free flap choice should be guided by an integrative three-dimensional matrix: defect characteristics×patient profile×institutional resources. The anterolateral thigh flap remains a workhorse for moderate to large defects because of its thickness, long pedicle, availability of fascia lata, and nerve harvest. The radial forearm free flap remains valuable for thin and pliable resurfacing of the lips, eyelids, nasal lining, and oral lining. The deep inferior epigastric perforator flap is useful for large-volume contour restoration. Additional soft tissue options-including the lateral arm, parascapular, and medial sural artery perforator flaps-should be considered when color match, donor-site morbidity, or body habitus makes traditional workhorse flaps suboptimal. Facial soft tissue reconstruction requires not only flap survival but also restoration of contour, sensation, oral competence, facial animation, donor-site acceptability, and patient-reported quality of life. Mature technologies such as CTA, selective ultrasound, virtual surgical planning, intraoperative indocyanine green angiography, and structured postoperative monitoring should be distinguished from evolving tools such as augmented reality, artificial intelligence decision support, robotic-assisted anastomosis, artificial vascular conduits, and allogeneic or xenogeneic transplantation. Future research should focus on multicenter registries, standardized outcome measures, cost-effectiveness analyses, and externally validated decision-support models.

Mature technologies such as CTA, selective ultrasound, virtual surgical planning, intraoperative indocyanine green angiography, and structured postoperative monitoring should be distinguished from evolving tools such as augmented reality, artificial intelligence decision support, robotic-assisted anastomosis, artificial vascular conduits, and allogeneic or xenogeneic transplantation. Future research should focus on multicenter registries, standardized outcome measures, cost-effectiveness analyses, and externally validated decision-support models.

title: Preoperative staging of gastric cancer: a prospective comparison of gastric filling ultrasonography and enhanced CT with implications for surgical decision-making.
abstract: Background Accurate preoperative staging is essential for optimizing treatment strategies in gastric cancer. While gastric-enhanced CT is widely used, its accuracy remains suboptimal, particularly for early-stage tumors. Gastric filling ultrasonography, a non-invasive technique using oral contrast to displace intraluminal gas, offers potential advantages in mural visualization. This prospective study compared the diagnostic performance of gastric filling ultrasonography and gastric-enhanced CT against postoperative pathological staging. Methods We enrolled 406 patients with histologically confirmed gastric cancer who underwent both imaging modalities prior to surgery. Preoperative T and N stages assigned by each modality were compared with pathological results. Diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and area under the ROC curve (AUC) were calculated. McNemar's test was used for paired comparisons, DeLong test for AUC comparisons, and Kappa statistics for agreement assessment. Univariate logistic regression identified factors affecting ultrasound accuracy. Results For T-staging, overall accuracy was 72.7% (295/406) for ultrasound vs. 63.5% (258/406) for CT ( P < 0.001). Ultrasound significantly outperformed CT in T1 (81.5% vs. 56.3%, P = 0.009) and T2 (81.1% vs. 67.9%, P < 0.001) stages. For N-staging, accuracy was 82.0% (333/406) for ultrasound vs. 60.1% (244/406) for CT ( P < 0.001). Kappa agreement with pathology was substantial for ultrasound T-staging ( κ = 0.625) and N-staging ( κ = 0.748), compared with moderate agreement for CT ( κ = 0.508 and 0.395, respectively). In multivariate analysis, vascular infiltration was the only independent factor associated with ultrasound T-staging accuracy. Conclusions Gastric filling ultrasonography demonstrates superior accuracy over gastric-enhanced CT for preoperative T1/T2 and N-staging, with substantial agreement with pathological findings. This non-invasive and radiation-free examination method can serve as an effective complement to CT, and is particularly suitable for gastric cancer at the T1 and T2 stages. We have proposed a complementary imaging protocol to assist in surgical decision-making, which is expected to enable clinicians to make more accurate preoperative staging assessments for patients with gastric cancer. Registration It was registered in the ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05596864).

title: Modern hysteroscopic management of congenital uterine anomalies: current techniques, emerging technologies, and future directions.
abstract: Background Congenital uterine anomalies are clinically relevant in reproductive medicine, particularly among women with infertility, recurrent pregnancy loss, adverse obstetric outcomes, or obstructive symptoms. Hysteroscopy has transformed the management of correctable intracavitary anomalies by enabling conservative, image-guided reconstruction of the uterine cavity while avoiding the morbidity of historical abdominal metroplasty. Scope This narrative review critically examines contemporary hysteroscopic management of septate uterus, dysmorphic uterus, bicorporeal septate uterus and rare obstructive malformations, such as Robert's uterus. We discuss the implications of the ESHRE/ESGE, CUME, and ASRM classification systems; the role of three-dimensional transvaginal ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging in preoperative mapping; and the technical principles that guide metroplasty, cavity remodeling, ultrasound-guided hysteroscopy, office-based metroplasty, and staged approaches in complex anatomy. Discussion Bipolar saline-based platforms, miniaturized resectoscopes, bipolar needle electrodes, cold scissors, and selected tissue removal systems have expanded the therapeutic spectrum and improved safety. The evidence supporting surgery remains heterogeneous: the TRUST randomized trial challenged routine septum resection in unselected women, whereas data for T-shaped and other dysmorphic uteri remain largely observational. Emerging technologies, including laser platforms, artificial intelligence-assisted hysteroscopy, and robotic concepts, are promising, but currently lack prospective validation. Conclusion Optimal management should therefore be individualized, anatomy-driven, and grounded in shared decision-making, with careful preservation of endometrium and myometrium. Standardized reporting, multicenter registries, and prospective comparative studies are needed to define which patients benefit most from hysteroscopic correction.

title: Pseudo-cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea following endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal surgery for PitNET: a case report and literature review.
abstract: Pseudo-cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhea, defined as non-CSF nasal discharge mimicking true CSF leakage, is a rare but clinically significant complication that may prompt unnecessary aggressive treatment. We report a case of a 64-year-old man who developed positional clear nasal discharge after endoscopic endonasal resection of recurrent pituitary neuroendocrine tumor (PitNET). Glucose oxidase testing was negative, and imaging demonstrated intact skull base reconstruction. Nasal endoscopy revealed bilateral crusting and purulent secretions without evidence of CSF leak. The condition was diagnosed as vasomotor rhinitis. Conservative management-including nasal debridement, antibiotic therapy, topical corticosteroids, and saline irrigation-led to complete symptom resolution. This case underscores the importance of differentiating pseudo-CSF rhinorrhea from true CSF rhinorrhea to avoid invasive interventions.

title: Age is the wrong axis: rethinking surgical selection for octogenarians with early-stage non-small cell lung cancer.
abstract: Lung cancer is increasingly a disease of older age, and as low-dose computed tomography screening extends into the ninth decade, a growing number of octogenarians present with early-stage, potentially curable non-small cell lung cancer. Faced with these patients, clinicians repeatedly ask a single question: is this patient too old for surgery? Recent prospective data show that selected octogenarians achieve long-term survival comparable to younger patients despite substantially higher complication rates, with quality of life that recovers over the first postoperative year. Yet the favorable result is attributed to careful selection that is rarely defined, and is seldom accompanied by any account of the patients who were assessed and not offered an operation. This article argues that chronological age is the wrong axis for the decision. Physiologic reserve, measurable through validated frailty instruments and established physiologic testing, predicts postoperative outcome far better than birth year, and aging is sufficiently heterogeneous that any age threshold misclassifies patients in both directions. A substantial competing risk of non-cancer death, compounded by overdiagnosis among screen-detected tumors, tempers the survival gain expected from aggressive treatment and makes overtreatment as real a hazard as age-based exclusion. A graded menu of options now exists, extending from minimally invasive lobectomy through sublobar resection and stereotactic ablative radiotherapy to active surveillance, and intensity should descend with reserve rather than with age. The task is to operationalize careful selection through structured geriatric assessment, multidisciplinary collaboration, prehabilitation, and shared decision-making, and to judge success by outcomes that older patients actually value.

title: Extended Reality for Image-Guided Small Animal Surgery: Current Evidence, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions.
abstract: Image-guided surgery has become an integral component of modern veterinary surgery using advanced imaging modalities, such as computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, ultrasonography, and fluoroscopy. Recently, extended reality (XR) technologies have emerged as promising tools to enhance image-guided surgical procedures by improving three-dimensional anatomical understanding, surgical navigation, and intraoperative decision-making. Although XR has gained considerable attention in human surgery, its application in veterinary surgery remains at an early stage. This narrative review aimed to provide a comprehensive overview of the current evidence regarding XR technologies in small animal surgery, with particular emphasis on their integration with preoperative and intraoperative imaging modalities. The available literature was reviewed to evaluate current clinical applications, technological developments and future perspectives. A literature search was performed in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published up to May 2026 using combinations of terms related to extended reality and small animal veterinary surgery. Original articles, case reports, pilot studies, technical reports, and reviews addressing clinical, experimental, or simulation-based applications were considered. Although several studies have explored the use of XR technologies for veterinary education, anatomical training, and diagnostic imaging instruction, relatively few investigations have assessed their direct application in clinical surgical practice. Potential applications have been described in orthopedic, oncologic, neurologic, cardiovascular, and minimally invasive procedures. Crucially, the currently available peer-reviewed evidence is restricted to canine patients, as no eligible feline studies were identified. Current evidence suggests that XR is an emerging technology with potential applications in canine surgical planning, image-guided procedures, and surgical training. Further prospective clinical studies are required to establish its clinical effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and impact on surgical outcomes.

title: Rat Calvarial Defect Models in Bone Regeneration Research: A Narrative Review of Critical Size and Micro-Computed Tomography Outcome Reporting.
abstract: The rat calvarial defect model supports the preclinical evaluation of bone-regenerative approaches relevant to craniofacial reconstruction, including recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein-2 (rhBMP-2) and bone substitutes. However, its invasive nature requires study-specific harm-benefit assessment and application of the 3Rs. This narrative review used a structured PubMed search to examine spontaneous healing in defects smaller than 5 mm and μCT outcome reporting in untreated or control defects. Twenty-four studies of sub-5 mm defects and 45 μCT studies were included. Complete spontaneous healing was not reported in the sub-5 mm studies; only two μCT studies reported regeneration of at least 50% according to their respective outcome measures. Healing generally increased with longer observation periods and smaller defects, although methodological heterogeneity limited comparisons. Inconsistent reporting of acquisition parameters, segmentation thresholds, regions of interest, and numerical outcomes restricted reproducibility and data reuse. Within this PubMed-indexed evidence base, the findings support 5 mm defects as a practical model of incomplete spontaneous healing and indicate that smaller defects also do not reliably heal completely within the observation periods studied. These findings do not directly establish clinical benefit. Future studies should justify the least burdensome model capable of answering the research question, implement replacement, reduction, and refinement, and report standardized bone volume fractions, relevant measures of defect bridging, reproducible imaging methods, and reusable numerical data.

title: MedNeXt-Based Automated Tumor Segmentation and TMTV Prognostication in Hodgkin Lymphoma PET Images: A Retrospective Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives : To evaluate a deep learning-based method for automatic segmentation of Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) on PET images and to explore the prognostic value of total metabolic tumor volume (TMTV) derived from segmentation. Methods : PET datasets from two independent institutions were retrospectively collected and divided into training and validation cohorts. MedNeXt was trained for HL PET segmentation and benchmarked against five representative segmentation architectures under the same data split, preprocessing pipeline, and evaluation framework. Segmentation performance was assessed using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), Jaccard index (JSC), 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95), and average symmetric surface distance (ASSD). Bland-Altman and linear regression analyses evaluated agreement between ground-truth TMTV (gtTMTV) and predicted TMTV (pTMTV). Cox proportional hazards regression analysis was applied to assess the prognostic value of pTMTV. Results : In the validation cohort, the mean values (±standard deviation) of DSC, HD95, JSC, and ASSD were 0.702 ± 0.191, 67.998 ± 99.220, 0.561 ± 0.203, and 16.992 ± 31.659, respectively. Among the evaluated segmentation models, MedNeXt showed the best segmentation performance. Mean gtTMTV and pTMTV were 424.681 ± 498.811 cm 3 and 405.871 ± 466.984 cm 3 , showing good agreement. pTMTV was significantly associated with progression-free survival (PFS) ( p = 0.048), but not overall survival (OS) ( p = 0.163). Conclusions : MedNeXt achieved reliable HL segmentation, although tumor boundary delineation requires further improvement. The derived pTMTV may serve as a prognostic indicator for PFS but showed no significant association with OS. Further validation in larger cohorts is warranted.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Feature Selection Algorithms for Predicting Radiation-Induced Complications in Head and Neck Cancer Using Multimodal CT and MRI Radiomics.
abstract: Head and neck cancer (HNC) presents a significant challenge due to its anatomic complexity and treatment-related complications such as sticky saliva and xerostomia, which critically impair patients' quality of life. Recent advancements in imaging technologies, using the concept of radiomics, offer promising approaches for predicting these complications and ultimately reducing their incidence. In this regard, robust feature selection is critical in radiomics-based predictive modeling due to the high dimensionality, redundancy, and instability of extracted imaging biomarkers. This study aims to evaluate nine distinct feature selection algorithms-Boruta, Kruskal, Recursive Maximum Relevance minimum redundancy (R-MRmr), Relief, Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE), Forward Selection (FS), Backward Elimination (BE), Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO), and Principal Component Analysis (PCA)-as a feature-transformation comparator for predicting sticky saliva and xerostomia in HNC patients using clinical, dosimetric, MRI and CT radiomics data. The study involved 250 HNC patients who underwent radiotherapy from three different institutions. From MRI and CT images, a total of 321 radiomic features (107 from each CT, T1, and T2-weighted MRI) along with 20 clinical and dosimetric features were extracted. The predictive robustness of feature selection methods was further evaluated across five machine-learning classifiers, including K-nearest neighbors (KNN), support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), logistic regression (LR), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), were initially benchmarked using a common feature selection procedure, after which SVM was selected as the reference classifier for systematic comparison of the feature-reduction approaches. Model performance was assessed using metrics objectives such as Area Under the Curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Among the evaluated feature selection approaches, R-MRmr and Relief generally yielded better discrimination, although performance varied according to toxicity endpoint and imaging modality. The highest AUCs were 0.85 for early sticky saliva (R-MRmr, T1-weighted MRI), 0.96 for early xerostomia (R-MRmr, T1-weighted MRI), 0.65 for late sticky saliva (Relief, combined CT+T1+T2), and 0.88 for late xerostomia (Relief, T1-weighted MRI). T1-weighted MRI frequently provided better individual-modality performance, whereas combining all three imaging modalities did not consistently improve discrimination. These findings demonstrate that the choice of feature selection strategy and imaging modality can materially influence radiomics-based toxicity prediction.

title: GammaTile<sup>®</sup> Brachytherapy as Spatially Fractionated Radiation Therapy for Postoperative Brain Cancer: A Paradigm for Precision Intracranial Radiotherapy.
abstract: Purpose: Tile-based radiation therapy (TBRT) delivers adjuvant radiation to brain tumor beds using evenly spaced cesium-131 (Cs-131) sources in collagen tiles. This study evaluated TBRT as spatially fractionated radiation therapy (SFRT) across tumor sizes and source counts. Methods and Materials: Dose distributions were generated from postoperative CT scans for 18 patients treated with TBRT, using 10-32 implanted Cs-131 sources per case (median, 20). The resection cavity (RC) was contoured on CT with registered postoperative T1-weighted MRI guidance. CTV_5mm was defined as the RC plus a 5 mm expansion excluding skull and surgical tract, and CTV_5mm_Eval as CTV_5mm minus the RC. Both volumes were analyzed using SFRT dose metrics from the Radiosurgery Society SFRT/Flash working group white paper, and planar high-dose core number density (HCND_A) was used to characterize TBRT spatial fractionation. Results : The mean dose indices of D5 (dose covering 5% of the target volume), D10, D50, D90, D95 and D100 were 175.8 ± 43.3, 148.8 ± 35.1, 86.7 ± 18.5, 56.1 ± 10.5, 50.2 ± 9.0 and 33.4 ± 7.2 Gy for the CTV_5mm_Eval, respectively. The heterogeneity indices, represented by the ratio of D5/D95 and D10/D90, were 3.5 ± 0.6 and 2.7 ± 0.4, respectively, which were in the range of the linac-based Lattice therapy. HCND_A was a constant, TBRT delivered one high dose core for every 1 cm 2 of tumor bed. All dose metrics in both the CTV_5mm and CTV_5mm_Eval were largely consistent across all plans. Conclusions : TBRT produced heterogeneous dose distributions comparable to conventional SFRT. A 60 Gy TBRT nominal prescription dose approximated the SFRT D90, or valley dose of the 5 mm expansion target volume, suggesting TBRT may provide an SFRT platform for tile-accessible cancers.

title: Cytoreductive Radical Prostatectomy in Oligometastatic Prostate Cancer and the Role of the Robotic Platform: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Background : Oligometastatic prostate cancer (OMPC) comprises biologically and clinically distinct states with a limited number of detectable metastases. Improved systemic therapy and prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PSMA PET/CT) have intensified interest in treating the primary tumor. Methods : In this narrative review we searched PubMed/MEDLINE from inception to 1 July 2026, reviewed current guidelines, and searched ClinicalTrials.gov, the ISRCTN registry and the EU Clinical Trials Register for ongoing surgical studies, prioritizing randomized trials, prospective studies, PSMA PET-staged cohorts, systematic reviews, guidelines, and studies of perioperative, functional and patient-reported outcomes. Results : Registry and institutional data generated the hypothesis that cytoreductive prostatectomy improves outcomes but are vulnerable to selection bias; prospective and PSMA PET-staged cohorts established feasibility. The phase II trial by Dai and colleagues supported radical treatment of the primary tumor but combined surgery and radiotherapy. RAMPP provided the first prostatectomy-specific randomized signal, with lower 5-year cancer-specific mortality after radical prostatectomy plus best systemic therapy than after systemic therapy alone (13% versus 23%; hazard ratio 0.39, 95% confidence interval 0.16-0.98), but accrual ended early, clinical progression was similar, overall survival was not significantly improved, systemic therapy predated contemporary intensification, and major surgery-related complications occurred in 14%. A randomized phase II trial with a predominantly surgical local-therapy arm found no progression-free or overall survival benefit, so randomized evidence is mixed. All randomized evidence concerns radical prostatectomy or local treatment irrespective of surgical approach; no trial has tested a robot-specific oncologic effect. Guidelines recommend prostate radiotherapy for selected low-volume de novo metastatic disease and restrict surgery to clinical trials. Conclusions : Cytoreductive prostatectomy, delivered mostly as robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP), is feasible and may improve local control while providing complete pathology, but it remains investigational; the robotic approach is the surgical platform, not a modality with distinct oncologic efficacy. Appropriate use requires expert-center surgery, modern staging, guideline-concordant systemic therapy, multidisciplinary selection, transparent counseling and, preferably, trial participation. Future trials must establish whether prostatectomy adds meaningful benefit beyond modern systemic therapy, prostate radiotherapy and metastasis-directed treatment, while measuring morbidity, continence and quality of life.

title: Worsening of Oral Health Parameters After Head and Neck Radiotherapy-Findings from a Multidisciplinary Head and Neck Tumor Board: A Prospective Observational Study.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate (a) changes in caries experience, (b) changes in periodontal status, and (c) the need for dental extractions in a cohort of patients treated with radiotherapy (RT) and chemoradiotherapy (RTCT) for head and neck cancer (HNC). Methods This prospective cohort study was approved by the local Ethics Committee (Ref. 22858/18) and registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (ID: NCT04009161). The study population consisted of patients with HNC who, prior to RT, underwent a dental examination followed by the elimination of oral foci of infection and were then enrolled in a follow-up program. The primary outcome was oral health worsening, defined as the onset of severe periodontitis and/or a DMFt score ≥ 13. Oral cavity RT dose was obtained contouring the 'buccal mucosa' organ at risk (OAR). Results In total, 113 patients were included (median follow-up: 44.77 months). The sample mainly included oral, oropharyngeal, nasopharyngeal and laryngeal cancers (89/113, 78.8%). Salivary glands, hypopharynx and other sites accounted for a minority of the cases (24/113, 21.2%). Seventeen patients (34.7%) experienced worsening of oral health status over time, which was associated with smoking (OR = 4.7, 95% CI: 1.27-17.37; p = 0.02). The DMFt index increased (difference: 4.08; 95% CI: 1.60-6.56; p = 0.001), and this increase was associated with smoking (β = 2.05, 95% CI: 0.27-3.83; p = 0.02). Although worsening of periodontitis stage was not statistically significant ( p = 0.35), localized deterioration was observed, with an increase in sites with PPD ≥ 5 mm ( p = 0.02). Forty-nine patients (43.4%) experienced tooth loss. Mean tooth loss was 2.12 teeth per patient ( p = 0.05), primarily due to caries (48.5%) and periodontitis (48.1%). Independent risk factors for tooth loss were age ( p = 0.025) and an RT dose > 60 Gy to the 'buccal mucosa' OAR ( p = 0.023). Conclusions Patients treated with RT experienced significant deterioration in dental and periodontal health, and oral cavity dosimetric parameters might be associated with tooth loss, although this association requires confirmation in further studies.

title: PET Tumour Segmentation in Head and Neck Cancer: Reproducibility, Reader Dependence and Concordance with CT-Defined Tumour Volume in a 154-Patient Cohort.
abstract: Purpose: Volumetric PET biomarkers carry substantial prognostic value in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), yet their clinical implementation is hampered by segmentation heterogeneity. A fundamental and unresolved question is which segmentation method is most suitable for routine clinical use, both for a reader experienced in PET segmentation and for a reader without PET segmentation experience, such as an ENT surgeon or a radiation oncologist. This study addressed this question by assessing the intra- and interobserver reproducibility of four PET segmentation methods in MIM Maestro Software Version 7.4.2, identifying tumour-related determinants of variability, and examining concordance between PET-derived metabolic tumour volume (MTV) and CT-based gross tumour volume (GTV). Methods: Two readers with contrasting PET segmentation experience, a nuclear medicine physician experienced in PET segmentation (R1) and an ENT surgeon without prior PET segmentation training (R2), applied four methods to the primary tumours of 154 patients with HNSCC (oral cavity, oropharynx, hypopharynx or larynx) treated with definitive (chemo)radiotherapy between 2010 and 2021: fixed absolute thresholds at SUV 3.0 and 4.0, a relative threshold at 41% of the maximum standardised uptake value (SUVmax), and a gradient edge-detection algorithm (PET Edge+). R1 segmented twice with a washout of at least 4 weeks; R2 performed one session and delineated CT-GTV in the 85 patients whose PET/CT-derived CT served directly as the radiotherapy planning scan. The second session of R1 served as the reference for all interobserver and MTV-GTV analyses. Agreement was assessed by ICC (two-way mixed model), coefficient of variation, repeatability coefficient and Bland-Altman analysis; determinants of variability by a multivariable linear mixed-effects model with a random intercept per patient. Results: All four methods demonstrated excellent intraobserver (ICC 0.993 to >0.999) and interobserver (ICC 0.989-0.996) reproducibility. SUV3.0 generated significantly more relative error than SUV41% (β = +3.1%; 95% CI 0.89, 5.3). PET Edge+ was the only method for which a significant method × reader interaction was observed in this reader pair: the reader without PET segmentation experience generated more error than the reader experienced in PET segmentation (β = +7.1%; 95% CI 3.9, 10), an effect concentrated in smaller tumours (below approximately 15 mL); in the 85-patient GTV subset, where tumours were larger on average, the interobserver ICC for PET Edge+ was 0.997. GTV concordance was good for three of four methods (ICC 0.808-0.895); SUV41% showed only moderate concordance (ICC 0.572). Conclusions: All four methods provided excellent volumetric reproducibility within a single clinical software platform, but they differed in reader dependence and in agreement with CT-defined GTV. Rather than supporting a universal segmentation standard, these findings suggest that the method should be selected according to its intended application, pending multicentre confirmation.
